final_notes:
Method/framework: 3-stage pipeline: construct persona steering vectors (RESGA rep diffs or SAE latent diffs), optimize prompts via EPO/gradient ascent away from persona, select/evaluate Pareto prompts. Earlier Fig.2 caption said 2 stages and Lλ=f+H, conflicting with Eq.4 Lλ=f−(λ/n)ΣCE. Objective uses last-token target-layer projection; earlier prompt-only optimization vs later context-aware dynamic batches.

Experiments: tasks sycophancy, TruthfulQA hallucination, myopic reward; metrics undesirable-option rates. Models Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 3 4B. Baselines zero-shot, standard prompt, dense steering, GCG, ProTeGi. Layers 25 Llama/Qwen, 20 Gemma. EPO M=100,n=8,T=1000; SAEGA K=20. Evaluation conditional log-prob. Earlier conflicts: Table 1 said two model families despite three; says lower better though sycophancy 50% is perfect neutralization.

Table 1/near conclusion: RESGA values 49.86, 50.63, 62.65, 45.12, 41.46, 51.22, 38.50, 38.50, 34.50; SAEGA 49.84, 49.95, 70.70, 46.95, 40.85, 49.14, 31.50, 40.50, 38.50. RESGA avg 45.83; SAEGA avg 46.44. Text claims sycophancy for both indistinguishable from 50, contradicted by Gemma 62.65/70.70.

Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19; text claims negligible/no disruption across all, but Qwen worsens ~15%. §4.4: RESGA may token-prime labels; SAEGA shifts vocab. Table 5 ablations: Random Direction, Random Mutation, Task Loss objective; all components matter. Limitations: require labeled persona/non-persona examples; SAE latents/vectors model-specific and need retraining; strongest prompts often semantically incoherent/fluency-effectiveness tradeoff. Broader impact: pipeline could be misused for SAE-latent jailbreak/harmful-output discovery; recommends access controls. Acknowledges Claude use for writing/code generation.

Title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors: Harshvardhan Saini (IIT ISM Dhanbad), Yiming Tang (NUS), Dianbo Liu (NUS); equal contribution indicated.

Abstract claims: Problem is controlling emergent behavioral personas in LLMs (examples: sycophancy, hallucination). Existing manual prompt engineering is intuitive but unscalable/imprecise; automatic optimization is effective but black-box. Proposed framework adapts gradient ascent to LLMs for targeted prompt discovery. Two methods: RESGA and SAEGA; both optimize randomly initialized prompts to better align representations with an identified persona direction. Introduces “fluent gradient ascent” to control fluency of discovered persona steering prompts. Demonstrates effectiveness across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3 for steering three personas: sycophancy, hallucination, and myopic reward. Abstract specifically says on sycophancy, automatically discovered prompts achieve “significant improvement (49.90% compared with 79.24%)” — wording may imply compare baseline/after but direction unclear; check later tables/results. Claims methods grounded in mechanistically meaningful features and provide controllable/interpretable behavior modification. Code repo link provided.

Title/authors: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Abstract: proposes gradient-ascent prompt discovery for persona control; two methods RESGA and SAEGA optimize randomly initialized prompts to align representations with identified persona direction; introduces “fluent gradient ascent”; evaluated on Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 3 for sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Abstract says sycophancy prompts achieve “significant improvement (49.90% compared with 79.24%)” (direction/meaning to check).

Intro/Fig.1: compares manual prompt steering, activation steering (inject dense vector v into representations e(t)), and RESGA/SAEGA deriving persona directions from contrastive activations and optimizing prompts via fluent gradient ascent for residual-based and interpretable feature-level control. Motivation: manual prompt engineering is unscalable; black-box auto prompt methods lack interpretability; SAEs/persona features enable interpretable latent control but inverse prompt discovery unexplored. Gradient ascent in LLMs difficult due discrete tokens/off-manifold projections; gradient-guided discrete optimization exists but not applied to model steering prompts.

Framework: RESGA = RESidual Gradient Ascent using dense residual stream representation differences. SAEGA = Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent using SAE latent-based approaches identifying causally relevant features. Both construct persona steering vectors capturing undesired behavioral traits, then use fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts that “steer away from target personas” with controllable fluency. Claims effectiveness on three tasks (sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward), with significant improvement specifically on sycophancy and myopic reward (Section 4.2), substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering methods. Also claims representation-level evidence that prompt-based steering avoids distributional shifts induced by dense steering, exposing limitation of dense steering.

steps.notes_before:
Method: Framework described as 3-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors for undesired traits using representation differences or SAE latents; (2) fluent gradient ascent to find prompts steering away from persona while fluent; (3) initialize/select prompts from Pareto frontier based on validation performance. But Fig.2 caption says 2 stages, omitting initialization/selection, and states objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with Eq.4.

3.1: RESGA representation vector: v_repr = mean e(x) over D+ persona-exhibiting examples minus mean e(x) over D− persona-free examples, at chosen layer. SAEGA: use pretrained SAE-Lens SAEs; compute latent relevance by mean activation difference persona vs persona-free; select top-K largest absolute differences I_K. v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i * (abar_i+ − abar_i−), where w_i is i-th row of W_enc and a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i).

3.2: Persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing points prompt representation away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq.4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); cross-entropy term penalizes low-probability sequences, encouraging interpretable prompts. Optimized with EPO: population M prompts, each with fluency weight λ_i, random or seed initialization, gradients wrt one-hot token encodings, select top-k candidate tokens by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate/select best per λ_i, periodic restarts retain best under random λ and reinitialize others. Produces Pareto frontier of fluency vs steering effectiveness.

Method/framework: described as 3-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors from representation differences or SAE latents; (2) fluent gradient ascent/EPO to find prompts steering away from persona while fluent; (3) initialize/select/evaluate prompts from Pareto frontier using validation performance. Fig.2 caption earlier said 2 stages and gave Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with Eq.4.

3.1: RESGA vector v_repr = mean e(x) on D+ persona examples − mean e(x) on D− persona-free examples at chosen layer. SAEGA: pretrained SAE-Lens SAEs; latent relevance = mean activation difference persona vs persona-free; select top-K by largest absolute differences I_K. v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i*(abar_i+−abar_i−), w_i row of W_enc, a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i).

3.2: Persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing moves prompt representation away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq.4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); cross-entropy penalizes low-probability/off-manifold sequences. EPO: population M prompts with λ_i; random or seed initialization; gradients wrt one-hot tokens; top-k candidate mutations by gradient magnitude; replace random token; evaluate/select best per λ_i; restarts retain best under random λ and reinitialize others. Produces Pareto frontier of fluency vs steering.

Current part: Initialization strategies: random uniformly sampled vocab, often fragmented/incoherent; seed initialization uses short natural phrase related to persona (e.g. “Please answer honestly”), giving higher-fluency Pareto regions without much loss of steering and preferred for interpretability. Candidate prompts are validated by appending to task inputs and measuring behavioral metric change. Fluency = model self cross-entropy, not necessarily readability/grammar; lower CE closer to training distribution, higher CE off-manifold. They report full Pareto frontier, emphasize intermediate prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity, assess stability across validation examples.

Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, Dianbo Liu; affiliations IIT (ISM) Dhanbad and NUS. Abstract claims problem: controlling emergent behavioral personas (sycophancy, hallucination) in LLMs. Existing methods: manual prompt engineering intuitive but unscalable/imprecise; automatic optimization effective but black boxes. Proposed framework adapts gradient ascent to LLMs for targeted prompt discovery. Two methods: RESGA and SAEGA; both optimize randomly initialized prompts to align representations with an identified persona direction. Introduces “fluent gradient ascent” to control fluency of discovered persona steering prompts. Demonstrated across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 3 for three personas: sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Abstract says on sycophancy automatically discovered prompts achieve significant improvement “(49.90% compared with 79.24%)” — note wording may imply improvement from/to these values but direction/metric unclear. Claims methods ground prompt discovery in mechanistically meaningful features. Code repo given: github.com/HarshSaini10/RESGA_SAEGA. Reviewed on OpenReview id dcmHPxgo4c.

Title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, Dianbo Liu. Abstract: proposes gradient-ascent prompt discovery for persona control; methods RESGA and SAEGA optimize randomly initialized prompts to align representations with an identified persona direction; introduces “fluent gradient ascent” to control fluency. Tested on Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 3 and personas sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Abstract says sycophancy prompts achieve significant improvement “(49.90% compared with 79.24%)” (direction/metric unclear). Code repo and OpenReview id noted.

Introduction/Figure 1: compares manual prompt steering, activation steering via dense vector v injected into representations e(t), and RESGA/SAEGA deriving persona directions from contrastive activations and optimizing prompts via fluent gradient ascent. Motivation: prompt engineering manual/unscalable; automatic prompt discovery black-box; mechanistic interpretability/SAEs can identify persona features but inverse prompt discovery unexplored. RESGA = residual stream dense representation approach; SAEGA = SAE latent/interpretable feature approach. Both first construct persona steering vectors capturing undesired behavioral traits: RESGA using direct representation differences; SAEGA using SAE latent-based causally relevant features. Then use fluent gradient ascent to discover prompts that “maximally steer away from target personas” with controllable fluency. Intro claims effectiveness on three tasks (sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward), with significant improvement on sycophancy and myopic reward (Sec 4.2), substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering methods; also representation-level evidence that prompt-based steering avoids distributional shifts caused by dense steering, exposing limitation of dense steering.

steps.notes_before:
Method: three-stage procedure: persona-vector construction, fluency-constrained discovery, initialization/frontier selection using validation performance. Fig. 2 says two-stage discovery from dense representations or sparse SAE latents, then optimized prompts; caption inconsistently writes L=f+H though Eq. 4 uses f - CE penalty.

Persona vectors: V7P/SAE uses SAE-Lens. For each latent, contrastive relevance = persona-positive minus persona-negative mean activation; choose largest absolute differences I_K. v_SAE = Σ_{i∈I_K} w_i(ā_i^+ - ā_i^-), with a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i), w_i row of W_enc. Direct QX2/representation vector v_repr = mean_{D+} e(x) - mean_{D-} e(x). D+ exhibits target persona, D- lacks it; e(x) activation at chosen layer. Suppression target direction v in activation space.

J4Z/fluent gradient ascent: objective f(t)= - <e(t),v>/||e(t)||, where e(t) is last-token representation at target layer; maximizing points representations away from target persona. Eq. 4 Lλ(t)=f(t) - (λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); λ trades steering and fluency. Algorithm 1 called N8C: maintains M candidates for different λ values, uses one-hot/token gradients for top-k substitutions, mutations, selection, restarts. It claims evolutionary search improves C7N D6V error by 23.50 points over E8U.

Initialization/selection: strongest steering prompts may be incoherent. Fluency is self-cross-entropy, not readability; lower CE = closer to model training distribution, higher = off-manifold. No hard threshold; analyze whole frontier. Natural-language seeds like “Please answer honestly” for B2R improve fluency without significant steering sacrifice. Select candidates by held-out validation behavior change; emphasize intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity increases; stability = consistent persona reduction across validation examples.

steps.notes_before:
Method: Framework described as 3-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors for undesired traits using representation differences or SAE latents; (2) fluent gradient ascent to find prompts steering away from persona while fluent; (3) initialize/select prompts from Pareto frontier based on validation performance. But Fig.2 caption says 2 stages, omitting initialization/selection, and states objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with Eq.4.

3.1: RESGA representation vector: v_repr = mean e(x) over D+ persona-exhibiting examples minus mean e(x) over D− persona-free examples, at chosen layer. SAEGA: use pretrained SAE-Lens SAEs; compute latent relevance by mean activation difference persona vs persona-free; select top-K largest absolute differences I_K. v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i * (abar_i+ − abar_i−), where w_i is i-th row of W_enc and a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i).

3.2: Persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing points prompt representation away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq.4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); cross-entropy term penalizes low-probability sequences, encouraging interpretable prompts. Optimized with EPO: population M prompts, each with fluency weight λ_i, random or seed initialization, gradients wrt one-hot token encodings, select top-k candidate tokens by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate/select best per λ_i, periodic restarts retain best under random λ and reinitialize others. Produces Pareto frontier of fluency vs steering effectiveness.

Current part: Initialization strategies: random uniformly sampled vocab, often fragmented/incoherent; seed initialization uses short natural phrase related to persona (e.g. “Please answer honestly”), giving higher-fluency Pareto regions without much loss of steering and preferred for interpretability. Candidate prompts are validated by appending to task inputs and measuring behavioral metric change. Fluency = model self cross-entropy, not necessarily readability/grammar; lower CE closer to training distribution, higher CE off-manifold. They report full Pareto frontier, emphasize intermediate prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity, assess stability across validation examples.

Method: Framework described as 3-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors for undesired traits using representation differences or SAE latents; (2) fluent gradient ascent to find prompts steering away from persona while fluent; (3) initialize/select prompts from Pareto frontier based on validation performance. But Fig.2 caption says 2 stages, omitting initialization/selection, and states objective Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with Eq.4.

3.1: RESGA representation vector: v_repr = mean e(x) over D+ persona-exhibiting examples minus mean e(x) over D− persona-free examples, at chosen layer. SAEGA: use pretrained SAE-Lens SAEs; compute latent relevance by mean activation difference persona vs persona-free; select top-K largest absolute differences I_K. v_SAE = sum_{i in I_K} w_i * (abar_i+ − abar_i−), where w_i is i-th row of W_enc and a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i).

3.2: Persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token representation at target layer; maximizing points prompt representation away from persona direction. Fluency objective Eq.4: Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ H(m(t≤i),t_{i+1}); cross-entropy term penalizes low-probability sequences, encouraging interpretable prompts. Optimized with EPO: population M prompts, each with fluency weight λ_i, random or seed initialization, gradients wrt one-hot token encodings, select top-k candidate tokens by gradient magnitude, mutate by replacing random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate/select best per λ_i, periodic restarts retain best under random λ and reinitialize others. Produces Pareto frontier of fluency vs steering effectiveness.

final_notes:
Title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” QX2=RESGA dense residual/persona directions; V7P=SAEGA causally relevant SAE latents. Objective suppresses undesired personas by moving prompts away from target direction, with fluency CE term; evolutionary/token-gradient search; seeds/frontier by validation.

Tasks: B2R sycophancy, U9K hallucination/TruthfulQA MC error, D6V myopic reward; lower undesirable-option fraction is better. Models C7N=Llama 3.1 8B, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B, F9S=Gemma 3 4B. Baselines include X5L, R3W, P8D, H2F, Z6Q. Layers C7N/W4X 25, F9S 20; M=100,n=8,T=1000; SAE L0≈50,K=20. B2R neutral/random=50%, neutral projection=0; baseline active SAE≈50, P8D>150, V7P 50–60.

Table 1 Avg: QX2 45.83 best, V7P 46.44, Z6Q 47.44. B2R: QX2 49.86/50.63/62.65, V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70 (F9S not neutral). U9K/D6V mixed; V7P best C7N D6V=31.50.

Part 6 qualitative claims: V7P sparse/semantic, near baseline L0, suppresses relevant SAE features, tight on-manifold PCA; P8D off-manifold feature explosion; QX2 partial mitigation. Table2 random-initialized QX2/V7P often gibberish. Table3 seed-initialized optimization lowers scores vs seeds. Table4 WikiText2 perplexity: C7N 12.56→12.07, W4X 10.88→12.48, F9S 30.51→29.19. Mechanisms: QX2 may exploit label/token priming/induction heads; V7P semantic/vocabulary shifts.

Part 7 claims: B2R V7P suppresses “Yes/True/Agree,” upweights “However/But”; D6V QX2/V7P upweight “Future/Long/Wait.” Table5 ablations: K3Y random direction and E8U random mutation worse; M5A task-loss objective unstable/underperforms most. Table5 QX2/V7P values match Table1 for listed cells.

Conclusion/limits: future work semi-supervised reduction of labeled data, cross-model transfer, multi-persona steering. Limitations: QX2/V7P need positive/negative persona examples; model-specific SAE latents/vectors require retraining; effective prompts often not semantically coherent. Broader impact: safety use but possible misuse/jailbreak/harmful elicitation.

Discovered prompts significantly improve B2R mitigation. Intro defines QX2=RESGA (RESidual Gradient Ascent): dense residual-stream optimization using direct representation differences to construct undesired-persona directions. V7P=SAEGA (Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent): latent-based optimization identifying causally relevant SAE features and constructing corresponding directions. Both maximize departure from these undesired-persona directions with controllable prompt fluency. Figure 1: manual prompts; activation steering injects dense vector v into representations e(t); QX2/V7P derive persona directions from contrastive activations and optimize prompts with J4Z, supporting residual-based and interpretable feature-level control. Intro claims automatically discovered prompts significantly improve B2R and D6V mitigation, substantially outperform manual prompting and dense steering; representation-level evidence shows dense steering causes distributional shifts avoided by prompt-based steering. Claims P8D preserves fewer active SAE features than V7P across every model. Background: prompt engineering is intuitive but expertise-heavy; automatic discovery often black-box. SAEs decompose activations into interpretable features; persona latents predict/control behavior; inverse discovery of prompts selectively activating task-relevant latents is underexplored. Continuous embedding optimization/projection can create off-manifold inputs; gradient-guided evolutionary token replacement used for adversarial/jailbreak prompts, not model-steering prompts. Code link: github.com/HarshSaini10/RESGA_SAEGA.

Title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors: Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, Dianbo Liu. Abstract/intro: QX2=RESGA (RESidual Gradient Ascent) optimizes randomly initialized prompts using dense residual-stream persona directions from contrastive representation differences; V7P=SAEGA (Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent) optimizes prompts using causally relevant SAE latent/features and corresponding directions. Both move away from undesired-persona directions with J4Z controlling discovered-prompt fluency. Evaluations span C7N, W4X, F9S and B2R, U9K, D6V. Claims discovered prompts significantly improve B2R/D6V mitigation and outperform manual prompting and dense activation steering; dense steering causes representation distributional shifts avoided by prompt-based steering. Claims P8D preserves fewer active SAE features than V7P across every model. Figure 1 contrasts manual prompts, activation steering (inject dense vector v into e(t)), and QX2/V7P prompt optimization from contrastive activations with J4Z for residual/feature-level control. Background: prompt engineering intuitive but expertise-heavy; automatic discovery often black-box; SAEs decompose activations into interpretable features/persona latents; inverse prompt discovery to activate task-relevant latents underexplored; continuous embedding/projection risks off-manifold inputs; gradient-guided evolutionary token replacement used for adversarial/jailbreak prompts, not model-steering prompts. Related work: RepE and CAA use contrast-pair/concept directions and inference-time activation addition; activation steering used for B2R, toxicity, bias; SAE persona features can predict/control misalignment through activation clamping. SAE architectures include JumpReLU, Top-K, Batch Top-K, Matryoshka. Prompt engineering related methods include N8C=EPO (gradient-guided evolutionary prompt optimization balancing objective/fluency), Z6Q=ProTeGi (API-generated criticism edits opposite semantic direction with beam/bandits), H2F=GCG (greedy coordinate gradient token substitution for target behaviors). Code link: github.com/HarshSaini10/RESGA_SAEGA.

Fluency objective Eq.4: maximize Lλ=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ cross-entropy next-token loss; lower self-cross-entropy = closer to training distribution. No hard fluency threshold; analyze frontier. Seeds like “Please answer honestly” for B2R improve fluency without significant steering sacrifice. Selection uses held-out validation behavioral metric; emphasize intermediate frontier and stability across validation examples.

Goal: suppress undesired personas by moving prompts away from target direction; J4Z fluency term.

Method: v_repr = mean e(D+) − mean e(D−). SAE vector uses top-K activation-difference latents: sum encoder rows weighted by mean activation differences. Objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token target-layer representation; optimize Lλ=f(t)−(λ/n)Σ next-token CE with evolutionary/token-gradient search. Seeds/frontier selected by held-out validation.

Experiments part 4: Tasks: B2R sycophancy, U9K hallucination/TruthfulQA multiple-choice error, D6V myopic reward; lower is better. Models: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S=Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Baselines: X5L zero-shot, R3W standard prompt, P8D dense steering, H2F logit optimization, Z6Q GPT-4o natural-language gradients/bandits/beam.

Implementation: layers C7N 25, W4X 25, F9S 20; M=100, n=8, T=1000; SAE natural L0≈50, K=20; B2R perfect neutralization=50%; neutral projection=0; baseline active SAE features≈50, P8D>150, V7P 50–60. Context-aware optimization appends candidates to task-specific training questions and uses combined sequence final internal state. Evaluation: choose higher logP(a|q,p); metric is fraction preferring undesirable option.

Table 1 Avg: QX2 45.83 best avg, V7P 46.44, Z6Q 47.44. B2R: QX2 49.86/50.63/62.65, V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70. U9K and D6V mixed; V7P best C7N D6V=31.50.

final_notes: Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Main claim: structured reasoning improves profile-consistent opinion modeling but does not remove bias. Method: task policy question q + persona p, predict stance; training data only final stances, no reasoning traces. Output schema reasoning+answer; GRPO reward=.25 format + .01 length + correctness. One model per unit/profile; no explicit persona representation except country label. SFT warm start: smartvote/ANES use synthetic positive/negative arguments per question from Llama 3.1 70B; earlier Fig.1 described SFT on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers. Datasets: WoM DE 6 parties Yes/Neutral/No train official WoM 2021–2025, test EU&I 2024 30 items; ANES 2020 79 items recoded Yes/Neutral/No, default conservative, 67 train/12 test, 21 respondents; Swiss smartvote 2023 75 items, 60 policy, four-point collapsed Yes/No, 18 candidates, 48 train/12 test. Table 3 best SFT+GRPO macro-F1: Llama 66.88/52.53/40.66; Qwen 65.11/49.38/38.44; Magistral 70.73/53.21/45.43. Llama SFT ANES 42.77 > SFT+GRPO 40.66, though conclusion says SFT+GRPO generally outperforms all baselines. Magistral best; ANES hardest; smartvote highest. SFT beats others for Right in smartvote and ANES. Bias: ANES Neutral recall worst; Right highest Neutral rate; negative correlation with Neutral rate; removing Neutrals improves F1 but Left–Right gap remains. PCA: agents imperfect; no overall left shift; right humans shift left, Left/Center right/conservative. Bias experiments: progressive hurts Right, conservative hurts Left; no consistent benefit to overrepresented group; Right more affected. Fig.7 inversion smartvote: Right benefits; Left/Center worse. Ethics says consistent underperformance on center/right, conflicting with WoM results. Reproducibility: code/datasets released; hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors at ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: study whether reasoning improves LLM opinion alignment for opinion modeling/political preferences. Motivation: RL has advanced mathematical reasoning; they train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Evaluation on three datasets covering U.S., European, and Swiss politics. Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors at ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: study whether reasoning improves LLM opinion alignment for opinion modeling/political preferences. They train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Evaluation on three datasets covering U.S., European/German, and Swiss politics. Main reported result: reasoning enhances opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias. GitHub release promised.

Introduction motivation: LLMs can generate political discourse but fail to reflect diversity of human political viewpoints. Existing opinion modeling mostly prompts with demographics/political affiliations and relies on demographic-opinion correlations; these methods allegedly fail at real distributions and are unstable. Paper instead seeks preference-consistent individual-level approach using known opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview-transcript persona methods perform well but are too costly; paper proposes using political survey/VAA data (ANES, voting advice applications) as structured opinion profiles. Claims surveys are common for bias evaluation/group simulation but not widely used for training individual-level political agents.

Method overview: use RL, specifically GRPO, treating opinion formation as reasoning. Agent writes short rationale and final choice; reward when final choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Contributions: (1) GRPO reasoning-based opinion alignment from survey responses; (2) benchmark on real-world political data: German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates; results show reasoning consistently improves alignment; (3) analyze ideological effects by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, revealing systematic performance variations across political spectrum.

Figure 1 says pipeline: first fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after fine-tuning model has correct format but not fully opinion-aligned; then use GRPO reward model rewarding proper formatting and correct answers.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Main claim: train LLM agents to produce profile-consistent answers via structured reasoning; evaluate on Swiss smartvote, German WoM, U.S. ANES; reasoning improves opinion modeling but does not remove bias.

Method details: task is policy question q + persona p (respondent/party/candidate), predict stance. Training data D={(p_j,q_i,y*_ij)} has only final survey stances, no reasoning traces. Output schema fixed: <reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. GRPO reward combines: format reward 1 per correctly placed tag, max 4; length reward -|L-L*|, max 0 at desired length; correctness reward indicator predicted answer equals ground truth. Total R = .25*format + .01*length + 1*correct. They state they do not use explicit persona representation and include only country label in system prompt; alignment to individuals comes solely through correctly answering questions. final_notes:
Method §3: survey opinion alignment; learn stance for q/persona from final labels only, output <reasoning>/<answer>. GRPO reward: format tags, length, correctness. No persona representation beyond country prompt. Optional SFT for CoT demos.

Datasets: smartvote CH 18 candidates, binary, 48 train/12 topic-stratified test; 2023 75 items/60 policy, 4-point collapsed Yes/No, 3 candidates per 6 parties. WoM DE 6 parties, Yes/Neutral/No, official 2021–2025 train, EU&I 2024 30 test. ANES 21 respondents, 3 per ideology point, 79 items recoded Yes/Neutral/No, 67/12 split.

Table 3: mean macro-F1 over 8 stochastic runs. Random baselines 50/33.33/33.33; majority 37.43/27.44/22.98. Best Magistral SFT+GRPO: 70.73 smartvote, 53.21 WoM, 45.43 ANES. SFT+GRPO generally best except Llama ANES: SFT 42.77 > SFT+GRPO 40.66.

§4.5–4.6: Llama SFT+GRPO ideology disparities; smartvote Left easier than Center/Right; WoM/ANES weaker. Right in smartvote/ANES: SFT outperforms other methods on avg. ANES Neutral hardest; Right highest Neutral base rate; performance negatively correlates with Neutral base rate. Removing Neutrals improves all groups but Left–Right gap remains; alternative recoding reduces Center/Right gap.

§4.7–4.9: smartvote PCA no overall left shift; agents shifted center-right/x and center/y; Right becomes more left-wing, Left/Center more right-wing/conservative. Biased SFT: progressive bias impairs Right; conservative bias impairs Left; underrepresented groups harmed, Right more. Synthetic inversion for Llama-3.1-8B: ≈180° PCA rotation; Right benefits, Left/Center worsen; Right after inversion still below original Left.

§5–Ethics: limitations include opinion noise, few profiles, scarce/nonaligned surveys; future persona reps, confidence/value head, Neutral handling. Conclusion/ethics: SFT+GRPO generally best; Neutral hard; ideological disparities, esp. center/right underperformance; caution deployment. Repro statement: code/datasets released; training hyperparams Appendix F; PCA details §E.5.

Intro details: Motivating question: digital twins voting faithfully; LLMs fail to reflect diversity. Current opinion-modeling mostly prompts with demographics/political affiliations and relies on correlations; authors seek preference-consistent approach using known individual opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview transcripts can model personas but are too costly; they propose political survey data (ANES and VAAs) as structured opinion representations. Claim surveys are common in bias/group simulation but not widely adopted for training individual-level political agents.

Method preview: Use RL, specifically GRPO, on survey data. Treat opinion formation as reasoning: model writes short rationale and final choice; reward when choice matches respondent answer, encouraging reasoning toward survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Figure 1 says pipeline: first fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after FT model has correct format but not fully aligned; then GRPO with reward model rewards proper formatting and correct answers.

Contributions: (1) GRPO RL for explicit reasoning/opinion alignment from survey responses. (2) Benchmark on three real-world political datasets: German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates; release as benchmark; claim results show reasoning consistently improves alignment. (3) Analyze ideological effects by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, revealing systematic performance variations across political spectrum.

Abstract claims: LLMs are candidates for modeling individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding. Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Abstract: LLMs may model individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting gives biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding. Structured reasoning trained via RL improves profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, Swiss politics; remains competitive with strong baselines; still leaves bias needing more mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. Methods/datasets released as research baseline; opinion models could help digital democracies shape fairer/popular policies.

Intro claims: Reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment. Survey-trained agents generate short rationales then choices; rewarded for matching respondent answers; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Motivation from recent RL gains (o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1). Digital twins voting on every issue require accurate political-behavior simulation and could improve election understanding/policy/democracy. LLM political discourse does not reliably represent viewpoint diversity. Demographic/affiliation prompts exploit correlations but miss real distributions and are unstable. Preference consistency uses known individual opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview-transcript personas perform well but are costly/impractical at scale. Large surveys and VAAs capture political positions, lack narrative/text richness, but structurally represent population opinions; used for bias evaluation/group simulation but less for individual-agent training. Contributions: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; released benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis of known-position individuals revealing systematic ideological variation in alignment quality. Figure 1: public surveys supply profiles; initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full opinion alignment; then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning.

Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Abstract/intro: naive prompting gives biased opinions; structured reasoning trained via RL improves profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, Swiss politics, though residual bias remains. Survey-trained agents generate short rationales then choices; rewards match respondent answers; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Digital-twin motivation; demographic/affiliation prompting unstable and misses distributions; preference consistency uses known individual opinions; interview personas perform well but costly. Contributions: QX2/GRPO-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis revealing ideological variation in alignment quality. Fig.1: public surveys supply profiles; initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full opinion alignment; then QX2/GRPO with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning.

Related work: persona adoption types—demographic, character, individualized; individual modeling most relevant but demographic dominates. Demographic prompting ranges from simple party affiliation to richer age/education/location and belief-network demonstrations; Stammbach et al. combine prompting with ORPO preference training. Limits: representativeness, steerability, consistency; groupwise accuracy unpredictable; overall distributions may miss subgroup variance and show prompt sensitivity. Beyond demographics: Park et al. use interviews for public-opinion surveys but require transcripts; Haller et al. provide respondent QA pairs in context for bias identification, not opinion modeling. Table 1 example: base prompt answers “No” to inequality-opportunity question; trained model gives rationale accepting some inequality with access to basic opportunities and final answer “A) Yes.” Reasoning section defines QX2 = GRPO, a PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization over multiple sampled outputs; math benchmarks show effectiveness. Yu et al. use persona/CoT prompting calibrated with M8C for vote aggregation, not RL/general preference profiles; present method could address but representative-sample modeling computationally prohibitive.

final_notes:
Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Structured reasoning QX2/GRPO improves profile-consistent answers on German-party R2V, U.S.-respondent M8C, Swiss-candidate J4Q; residual bias remains. Stances generally {No, Neutral, Yes}; J4Q binary {Yes, No}. Rewards: format max4, length=-|L-L*|, correctness=1 if match; weights .25/.01/1. V7K=SFT synthetic CoT; ZP4=SFT+GRPO.

Datasets: J4Q smartvote 2023: 18 candidates, 6 parties, 60 Q/12 topics, 48 train/12 test. R2V Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025: 6 parties; labels Yes/Neutral/No; OOD B5X EU&I 2024 test 30. M8C ANES 2020: 21 respondents, 79 items, 67 train/12 test; labels via I7V conservative mapping, O2K aggressive robustness; 3 respondents per LC self-placement answer. §4.2 says 47 models trained, but unit counts imply 45.

Backbones: T9A=Llama3.1 8B non-reasoning; K6Y=Qwen3 8B and W2E=Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained. Table 3: D3G macro-F1 means/std over 8 stochastic runs T=1.0; baselines C6W=random, U9F=majority, H3D=ICL, N8R Stammbach hyperparams.

Results: ZP4 beats naive/V7K except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q, better on R2V. J4Q highest, M8C hardest; Neutral difficult. Native reasoning no consistent gain; W2E best overall. Ideology: P7N best in J4Q; centrist/right-leaning harder; X8J often hard. Neutral rate negatively correlates with F1/accuracy; removing Neutral improves/narrows gaps. Representation: no overall left shift; center-right/centerward distortions. Biased init and inversion show asymmetric ideology-learning difficulty.

Conclusion/ethics: claims ZP4 generally outperforms all baselines; warns of centrist/right-wing underperformance, neutral difficulty, and deployment/fairness risks. Reproducibility: code/data GitHub ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; docs include hyperparams, PCA details/results in E.5, per-party counts, recoding, sample-size and inversion details.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Main claim: structured reasoning training improves profile-consistent stance prediction but does not remove bias. Conclusion: persona-conditioned agents trained on known opinions with structured reasoning; across smartvote, Wahl-o-Mat, ANES, SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; Neutral stances remain challenging; accuracy varies significantly across political spectrum.

Method: per-profile/agent training; input policy question + persona/profile/country; output <reasoning> and <answer>. Training uses final stances only, no reasoning traces. GRPO reward = .25 format + .01 length + correctness. SFT warm start on synthetic arguments for positive/negative stances generated by Llama 3.1 70B plus ground-truth answers.

Datasets: WoM DE six parties, Yes/Neutral/No, official WoM 2021–2025 train, EU&I 2024 30 test. ANES 2020: 79 items recoded Yes/Neutral/No; default conservative; 67 train/12 test; 21 respondents. Swiss smartvote 2023: 60 binary Yes/No items; 18 candidates; 48 train/12 test.

Models: Llama3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B. Table 3 best SFT+GRPO: Llama 66.88/52.53/40.66, Qwen 65.11/49.38/38.44, Magistral 70.73/53.21/45.43 for smartvote/WoM/ANES. Smartvote easiest/highest; ANES hardest/lowest.

Ideology/bias: Left better than Center/Right on smartvote; WoM Left/Center roughly equal and Right relatively strong. ANES Neutral recall worst; neutral base rate harms F1/accuracy. PCA: agents shift center/right/conservative-liberal center; Right move left, Left/Center move right/conservative. Biased SFT: progressive hurts Right, conservative hurts Left; underrepresented group shifts/harmed most; conservative-biased and default SFT displacement similar. Inversion smartvote: flipping labels worsens Left, improves Right but still worse than Left. Ethics later incorrectly says “consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles,” conflicting with WoM results.

Limitations/future: opinion noise, few profiles, scarce surveys; single model with compact personas; uncertainty handling esp. Neutral. Reproducibility: code/datasets at GitHub; hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details Section E.5.

Introduction motivation: LLMs can generate political discourse but fail to reflect diversity of human political viewpoints. Existing opinion modeling mostly prompts with demographics/political affiliations and relies on demographic-opinion correlations; these methods allegedly fail at real distributions and are unstable. Paper instead seeks preference-consistent individual-level approach using known opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview-transcript persona methods perform well but are too costly; paper proposes using political survey/VAA data (ANES, voting advice applications) as structured opinion profiles. Claims surveys are common for bias evaluation/group simulation but not widely used for training individual-level political agents.

Method overview: use RL, specifically GRPO, treating opinion formation as reasoning. Agent writes short rationale and final choice; reward when final choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Contributions: (1) GRPO reasoning-based opinion alignment from survey responses; (2) benchmark on real-world political data: German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates; results show reasoning consistently improves alignment; (3) analyze ideological effects by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, revealing systematic performance variations across political spectrum.

Related work: persona adoption types—demographic, character, individualized; individual modeling most relevant but demographic dominates. Demographic prompting ranges from simple party affiliation to richer age/education/location and belief-network demonstrations; Stammbach et al. combine prompting with ORPO preference training. Limits: representativeness, steerability, consistency; groupwise accuracy unpredictable; overall distributions may miss subgroup variance and show prompt sensitivity. Beyond demographics: Park et al. use interviews for public-opinion surveys but require transcripts; Haller et al. provide respondent QA pairs in context for bias identification, not opinion modeling. Table 1 example: base prompt answers “No” to inequality-opportunity question; trained model gives rationale accepting some inequality with access to basic opportunities and final answer “A) Yes.” Reasoning section defines QX2 = GRPO, a PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization over multiple sampled outputs; math benchmarks show effectiveness. Yu et al. use persona/CoT prompting calibrated with M8C for vote aggregation, not RL/general preference profiles; present method could address but representative-sample modeling computationally prohibitive.

Table 3 D3G=macro-F1, T=1, 8 runs. ZP4 generally best: T9A 66.88/52.53/40.66; K6Y 65.11/49.38/38.44; W2E 70.73/53.21/45.43 on J4Q/R2V/M8C. Section 4.3 says ZP4 beats naive and V7K except T9A on M8C; J4Q higher due binary labels, R2V > M8C due more training, but also inconsistently says M8C peaks highest/J4Q hardest.

Ideology: T9A/ZP4 J4Q P7N > A4U/X8J; R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal; M8C lower. V7K best for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual. Representation: no overall left shift; agents shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; X8J more left, P7N/A4U more right/conservative. Biased initialization harms underrepresented views; inversion helps X8J, worsens P7N/A4U. J4Q inversion flips all answers, trains T9A, compares before/after F1; inversion rotates positions ~180°, right-wing ↔ left-wing. Fig. 7: P7N worsens; X8J improves but remains below P7N.

Discussion: limitations include same-respondent day-to-day noise, per-profile training computational cost/few agents, scarce suitable surveys/low items/generic themes/misaligned cross-country questions. Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors at ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: study whether reasoning improves LLM opinion alignment for opinion modeling/political preferences. Motivation: RL has advanced mathematical reasoning; they train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Evaluation on three datasets covering U.S., European, and Swiss politics. Main reported result: reasoning enhances opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias. They release method and datasets at GitHub link.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors at ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: study whether reasoning improves LLM opinion alignment for opinion modeling/political preferences. They train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Evaluation on three datasets covering U.S., European/German, and Swiss politics. Main reported result: reasoning enhances opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias. GitHub release promised.

Introduction motivation: LLMs can generate political discourse but fail to reflect diversity of human political viewpoints. Existing opinion modeling mostly prompts with demographics/political affiliations and relies on demographic-opinion correlations; these methods allegedly fail at real distributions and are unstable. Paper instead seeks preference-consistent individual-level approach using known opinions rather than demographic proxies. Interview-transcript persona methods perform well but are too costly; paper proposes using political survey/VAA data (ANES, voting advice applications) as structured opinion profiles. Claims surveys are common for bias evaluation/group simulation but not widely used for training individual-level political agents.

Method overview: use RL, specifically GRPO, treating opinion formation as reasoning. Agent writes short rationale and final choice; reward when final choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Contributions: (1) GRPO reasoning-based opinion alignment from survey responses; (2) benchmark on real-world political data: German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates; results show reasoning consistently improves alignment; (3) analyze ideological effects by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, revealing systematic performance variations across political spectrum.

Figure 1 says pipeline: first fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after fine-tuning model has correct format but not fully opinion-aligned; then use GRPO reward model rewarding proper formatting and correct answers.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Abstract/main claims: train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning; evaluate on three datasets covering U.S., European/German, and Swiss politics; reasoning enhances opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines but does not fully remove bias; GitHub release promised.

Intro/method: LLM political opinion modeling via demographics is unstable and fails to reflect real distributions/diversity. Paper proposes individual-level preference-consistent agents using known opinions from political surveys/VAAs rather than demographic proxies or costly interview transcripts. Uses RL/GRPO treating opinion formation as reasoning: model writes short rationale then final choice; reward for correct final choice matching respondent. Figure 1 pipeline: SFT on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers to learn reasoning template/format, then GRPO rewards formatting and correct answers. Contributions include benchmark on German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates, and ideological analysis by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions.

Related work part: distinguishes demographic, character, individualized personas; individualized is most relevant but rare. Demographic prompting includes simple affiliation, richer demographics, belief-network demonstrations, demographics+demonstrations, ORPO. Limitations from Santurkar: representativeness, steerability, consistency; models may approximate aggregate distributions but miss subgroup variance and are prompt-sensitive. Individual profile work: Park et al. interview transcripts strong but limited availability; Haller et al. in-context QA pairs for respondents, focused on bias identification. Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Main claim: train LLM agents to produce profile-consistent answers via structured reasoning; evaluate on Swiss smartvote, German WoM, U.S. ANES; reasoning improves opinion modeling but does not remove bias.

Method details: task is policy question q + persona p (respondent/party/candidate), predict stance. Training data D={(p_j,q_i,y*_ij)} has only final survey stances, no reasoning traces. Output schema fixed: <reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. GRPO reward combines: format reward 1 per correctly placed tag, max 4; length reward -|L-L*|, max 0 at desired length; correctness reward indicator predicted answer equals ground truth. Total R = .25*format + .01*length + 1*correct. They state they do not use explicit persona representation and include only country label in system prompt; alignment to individuals comes solely through correctly answering questions. Optional SFT warm start uses chain-of-thought demonstrations in exact format to ease format learning and initialize political reasoning. Earlier notes said Figure 1 described SFT on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers.

Datasets/Table 2: smartvote CH unit=candidate, #units 18, labels {Yes, No}, train Q 48, test Q 12 topic-stratified. WoM DE unit=party, #units 6, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, train Q see Table 5, test Q 30 (EU&I). ANES 2020 US unit=respondent, #units 21, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, train Q 67, test Q 12 random. Earlier Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B trained on individual in Right ANES; base prompt answered No but SFT+GRPO answered A) Yes.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Main claim: train LLM agents to produce profile-consistent answers via structured reasoning; evaluate on Swiss smartvote, German WoM, U.S. ANES; reasoning improves opinion modeling but does not remove bias.

final_notes: Methods/results retained: C6W=random uniform; U9F=unit training-set majority; H3D=ICL with same-topic train Q-A pairs; N8R uses Stammbach hyperparams. ZP4 generally best: beats naive/V7K except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q highest due binary/no Neutral; M8C hardest; R2V > M8C due more training. Native reasoning not consistently helpful: T9A > K6Y on R2V/M8C; W2E best overall; QX2 alone trails ZP4. Neutral-containing datasets worse. Ideology/group disparities: ZP4 usually best, but training methods underperform on centrist/right-leaning groups. T9A/ZP4 group F1: J4Q P7N clearly > A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C similar weaker. V7K averages exceed all methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral: M8C Neutral recall worst; X8J highest Neutral rate; removing Neutral improves all but P7N–X8J remains. Fig4: M8C Neutral base rate vs F1/accuracy strong negative correlations significant 5%. Representation/J4Q PCA: no overall left shift; X8J agents more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing/conservative. Biased init: progressive args harm X8J, conservative harm P7N; harm underrepresented more than help overrepresented. Synthetic inversion flips every J4Q answer, roughly 180° PCA rotation converting right-wing to left-wing and vice versa; trains T9A on flipped data. X8J benefits; P7N/A4U worsen; inverted X8J still below original P7N. Possible inconsistency noted earlier: authors say inversion supports harder right-wing learning despite P7N converting right-to-left and worsening. Conclusion/ethics reiterate ZP4 generally outperforms baselines, Neutral difficulty, political-spectrum accuracy variation, centrist/right-wing underperformance, and caution against deployment until fairness resolved. Reproducibility states code/datasets at GitHub and docs include training details/hyperparams, PCA details (Section E.5), per-party counts, recoding definitions, training-size analysis, inversion details.

Related work notes: demographic/persona prompting unstable; individualized modeling most relevant; interviews costly. Table 1 example: trained model answers inequality-opportunity question “A) Yes” with rationale.

Method §3: Given question q, persona p (respondent/party), stance set stated as Y={No, Neutral, Yes}; individual alignment learns p’s stance. §3.1 says only country label in system prompt, no explicit persona representation; training observations D={(p_j,q_i,y*ij)} contain final stances but no reasoning. Model must output `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. Reward = alpha1 E6Z format + alpha2 F2B length + alpha3 G9L correctness. E6Z: 1 per correctly placed tag, max 4; F2B=-|L-L*| max 0; G9L=1 if predicted answer matches ground truth. Weights alpha1=.25, alpha2=.01, alpha3=1. Optional SFT/V7K constructs CoT demos in exact rewarded schema, improving initial reasoning and reducing format burden.

Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Claim: structured reasoning trained via QX2/GRPO improves profile-consistent answers across German-party, U.S.-respondent, Swiss-candidate politics; residual bias remains. Method: stance set generally {No, Neutral, Yes}; J4Q binary {Yes, No}. One model per unit; output `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. Rewards: format E6Z, length F2B, correctness G9L; SFT/V7K builds CoT demos, ZP4=SFT+GRPO.

Data: J4Q smartvote 2023 English Swiss questionnaire: 75 items incl. 60 policy over 12 topics; 18 candidates (3 from each of 6 parties); Likert collapsed to Yes/No; one question/topic held out = 12 test, 48 train. R2V/Wahl-O-Mat: German parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD; 2021–2025 positions; labels Yes/Neutral/No; B5X EU&I 2024 OOD test with 30 items. M8C/ANES 2020: 79 policy items after exclusions; 21 respondents, 3 per liberal-conservative answer option; labels via I7V conservative mapping unless stated, O2K aggressive alternative; random split 67 train/12 test.

J4Q highest due binary/no Neutral; M8C hardest; R2V > M8C due more training. Native reasoning not consistently helpful: T9A > K6Y on R2V/M8C; W2E best overall; QX2 alone trails ZP4, implying SFT init helps. Neutral-containing datasets worse.
Fig3/ideology: ZP4 usually best, but all training methods underperform on centrist/right-leaning groups. T9A/ZP4 group F1: J4Q P7N clearly > A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C similar weaker, R2V P7N≈A4U, M8C lower. Fig4: M8C T9A/ZP4 Neutral base rate vs F1/accuracy strong negative correlations significant 5%.
Representation/J4Q PCA: no overall left shift; shifts center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; overall conservative negative-y trend; X8J agents more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing/conservative. Biased init: progressive args harm X8J, conservative harm P7N; harm underrepresented more than help overrepresented; S5Q=Llama3.3 70B generated biased argument sets. Synthetic inversion: X8J benefits; P7N/A4U worsen; inverted X8J still below original P7N, suggesting left profiles may be intrinsically easier.

Motivation: RL has advanced mathematical reasoning; they train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Abstract/main claim: study whether reasoning improves LLM opinion alignment for political/opinion modeling; train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning; evaluation on 3 datasets covering U.S., European/German, and Swiss politics; reasoning enhances opinion modeling/competitive with baselines but does not fully remove bias; release method/datasets at GitHub.

Intro motivation: LLMs can generate political discourse but fail to reflect diversity of human viewpoints; existing opinion modeling often prompts with demographics/party affiliation, relying on correlations and unstable across prompts/groups. They propose preference-consistent approach using an individual’s known opinions, not demographic proxies. Surveys/VAAs provide scalable structured political opinions; interviews richer but costly. Surveys widely used for bias/group simulation but not widely for training individual-level political agents.

Method overview: Use RL, specifically GRPO, treating opinion formation as reasoning. Agent writes short rationale + final choice; reward when choice matches respondent’s answer on unseen questions. Figure 1: first fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after fine-tuning model formats correctly but not fully aligned; then GRPO with reward model rewards formatting and correct answers.

Contributions claimed: (1) RL/GRPO for reasoning-based opinion alignment from survey responses. (2) Benchmark on three authentic political opinion datasets: German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates; reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment. (3) Analyze ideological effects by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions; claim answer inversion improves Left profiles but harms Right profiles.

Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Main claim: reasoning/RL improves LLM opinion alignment for political/opinion modeling across 3 datasets: U.S./ANES voters, European/German parties, Swiss candidates; competitive but not bias-free. Method: preference-consistent individual opinion profiles from known answers, not demographic proxies. Agent writes short rationale + final choice; reward if final choice matches respondent on unseen questions. Pipeline: SFT on synthetic statements/ground-truth answers to enforce reasoning template, then GRPO with rewards for formatting and correctness. Contributions include GRPO for reasoning-based opinion alignment; benchmark on authentic political datasets; ideological analysis via answer inversion, claimed to improve Left profiles but harm Right profiles.

Related work: prior political opinion modeling mostly demographic personas (party, age/education/location, etc.), with limitations of representativeness, steerability, consistency, subgroup variance, prompt sensitivity. Individualized persona work is rare: Park et al. use interview transcripts with strong survey accuracy but limited by transcript availability; Haller et al. use in-context respondent Q-A pairs to predict test answers but focus on bias identification. Reasoning training background: CoT/“think step by step,” training/search/RL for reasoning; GRPO is PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization without value function, normalizing rewards within sampled output group.

Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B trained on an ANES individual in Right group. Question: “Do you agree that it is not really that big a problem if some people have more of a chance in life than others?” Before base prompting answered No using equal opportunity fairness; after SFT+GRPO gave reasoning about inequality/incentives/basic necessities and final `<answer>A) Yes</answer>`. Caption says before training Llama disagreed; after training it agreed, while reasoning appealed to similar “equal opportunity” arguments framed differently.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: LLMs are candidates for modeling individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding. Structured reasoning trained through reinforcement learning produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics; remains competitive with strong baselines; but still leaves bias requiring additional mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: LLMs can model individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding. Structured reasoning trained through RL produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics; remains competitive with strong baselines; still leaves bias needing more mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. Methods/datasets released; opinion models could help digital democracies.

Intro claims: reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment. Survey-trained agents generate short rationales followed by choices; rewards for matching respondents’ answers; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Motivation from RL reasoning gains (o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1). Digital twins require accurate political-behavior simulation. Demographic/affiliation prompts exploit correlations but miss real distributions and are unstable; preference consistency uses known individual opinions. Interview transcripts can give strong persona performance but are costly. Large surveys and Voting Advice Applications capture political positions but lack narrative richness; used for bias evaluation/group simulation, less for individual-agent training.

Stated contributions: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; released benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis of individuals with known positions showing answer inversion improves P7N profiles but harms X8J profiles. Figure 1: public surveys supply individual profiles; initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements and ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full opinion alignment; then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning.

Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Abstract/intro claim reasoning improves profile-consistent political opinion alignment across U.S., European, Swiss politics, though residual bias remains. Method: survey-trained agents generate short rationales then choices; rewards for matching respondents. Contributions: QX2/GRPO-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis: inversion improves P7N profiles but harms X8J profiles. Figure 1: public surveys supply individual profiles; initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements/ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full alignment; then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning.

Related work: political personas include demographic, character, individualized; individual modeling most relevant but rarer. Demographic prompting ranges from party prompts to age/education/location, belief-network demonstrations, demographics plus demonstrations, and ORPO preference training (N8R) for target positions. Demographic limitations: representativeness, steerability, consistency; group accuracy unpredictable, subgroup variance missing, prompt sensitivity. Interview-based individualized profiles outperform demographic baselines but require transcripts; in-context respondent Q&A used mainly for bias identification.

After ZP4 reasoning accepts some inequality as inevitable/necessary while stressing basic necessities/opportunities; final answer A) Yes. Caption says training changes disagreement to agreement while retaining equal-opportunity arguments under different framing.

Training reasoning section defines QX2 = GRPO, a PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization: sample multiple outputs, subtract reward mean, divide by reward SD. Reasoning for alignment: Yu et al. use persona CoT prompting calibrated with M8C for voting, not RL/general preference profiles; present method could address but representative-sample modeling is computationally prohibitive.

Title: IA2 alignment with ICL activations improves SFT. Method: collect response-token activations from ICL/base with demos, train no-demo model to match (IA2), then SFT on ground truth; Qwen3-4B/Llama, LoRA r8, N up to 16 Llama/8 Qwen, IA2 G=200. Earlier claims: ICL/base vs SFT/no-demo activations low similarity; ICL better calibrated; higher activation similarity improves calibration, but extreme alignment may hurt accuracy; related work says authors found SFT worse than ICL.

Table2 Qwen N=4 multi-token: IA2→SFT beats SFT-only on all listed accs, but GSM8K IA2-only 77.4 > IA2→SFT 73.6; IA2→SFT sometimes worse than ICL. Table3 Qwen N=4 on ICL responses: GSM8K SFT 66.4, IA2 77.4, IA2→SFT 67.2, IA2+SFT 77.0; text says IA2+SFT > SFT-only. KD Table4: Llama GSM8K N=4 IA2+SFT 37.0 vs soft labels 36.1; SST2 N=8 IA2+SFT acc 66.9 but ECE .28 worse than soft .16.

Table5 Qwen math: GSM8K N=2/4/8 ICL 81.2/76.4/77.2, SFT 65.2/70.9/73.5, IA2 70.7/77.4/78.8, IA2→SFT 74.6/73.6/76.0; HMathA IA2→SFT > SFT. Table6 (IA)3 Llama N=4: IA2→SFT acc > SFT and ICL in all listed rows. Conclusion claims IA2 consistently improves accuracy/calibration of SFT, contradicted by Table1 exceptions. Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Abstract claims: SFT trains weights for target responses; ICL adapts at inference via prompt instructions/demonstrations. ICL can have better generalizability and calibration than SFT in data-scarce settings but higher inference compute. Authors claim they show ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns, implying different functional mechanisms. They introduce ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation technique to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. IA2 is performed as a priming step before SFT and is claimed to significantly improve accuracy and calibration across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families. Need check later for consistency with: 12 benchmarks, two model families, IA2 as priming before SFT, improvements in both accuracy and calibration, and claims about distinct activation patterns.

Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Abstract/introduction claims: SFT adapts weights to labeled samples; ICL adapts at inference via prompt demonstrations/instructions. ICL generalizes well in few-shot and is well calibrated, but costs context/inference compute. SFT can overfit/shortcut in few-shot and be miscalibrated/subpar. Authors claim ICL and SFT with same data can look similar in token/output space but produce disparate internal activations, indicating different functional mechanisms (§3). Hypothesis: ICL activations contain rich information about extracting generalizable patterns from context, absent in few-shot SFT.

IA2 = ICL Activation Alignment, a self-distillation/priming method: (1) collect information-rich ICL activations, (2) enforce functional alignment with ICL by matching activations, then (3) perform SFT on the primed model using same data. Claimed to improve SFT performance/quality and calibration across text classification and generation tasks. Abstract says across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families; intro says trained over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks. Need check later for two model families and calibration results.

Contributions to verify later: (1) ICL and SFT with same data do not align in activation space; (2) IA2 priming before SFT drastically improves performance; (3) IA2 training signal is not present in SFT-only training and is important. Figure 1 described as showing standard SFT enforces output-space alignment only and IA2 matches rich ICL activation patterns; comparison charts aggregated across models/datasets in §5.

§2 definitions: Decoder-only transformer LM M_Θ; self-attention uses W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O (W_QKVO). SA output per token z_i = softmax(q_i K^T/sqrt(d)) V · W_O, with q_i=t_i W_Q, K=t_:i W_K, V=t_:i W_V; Z same shape R×d as T. SFT dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}_{i=1}^N; weights Θ→Θ′; for response Y_i of G tokens, loss L_SFT=sum_i sum_j CE(̄Y_ij,Y_ij). ICL prompts original M_Θ with demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘...∘X_n∘Y_n] plus test X_t, no weight updates, output M_Θ(I∘X_t)=ŷ_t; paper focuses on classic input-output demo ICL. Activations = hidden SA outputs. For L layers and R tokens, activation tensor A size L×R×d. They study T=[I∘X] for ICL and T=X without ICL under different weights. Activation similarity asim(A1,A2)=token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors, size L×R (requires comparable token dimensions).

Paper title/claim: IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) improves supervised fine-tuning. Abstract says SFT trains weights for target responses; ICL adapts at inference via prompt demos/instructions and can generalize/calibrate better in data-scarce settings but with more inference compute. Authors claim they first show ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns, suggesting different functional mechanisms. They introduce IA2, a self-distillation technique to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. IA2 is performed as a priming step before SFT and is claimed to significantly improve accuracy and calibration on 12 popular benchmarks and two model families.

Title/claim: IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) improves SFT. Abstract: SFT trains weights for target responses; ICL adapts at inference via demos/instructions, can generalize/calibrate better in data-scarce settings but costs inference/context. Authors claim first to show ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns, suggesting different mechanisms; IA2 self-distills/replicates ICL activation patterns in SFT models, encouraging ICL-like internal reasoning. IA2 is a priming step before SFT and is claimed to significantly improve accuracy and calibration on 12 popular benchmarks and two model families.

Intro details: SFT adapts LLMs using labeled samples; PEFT makes SFT models small/loadable, but SFT often needs many labels. ICL uses query preceded by demos/instructions; prior work and their §5 experiments say ICL generalizes well few-shot and is typically well calibrated, but uses context/inference cost. They claim token-space behavior of ICL/SFT may look similar, but activations differ (§3), implying functional difference. Hypothesis: ICL activations contain rich information for extracting generalizable patterns; SFT may lack this, especially few-shot, due to shortcut learning/overfitting. IA2: (1) collect ICL activations, (2) enforce functional alignment with ICL, (3) perform SFT on primed model. They claim IA2 before SFT using the same data drastically improves performance on text classification and generation tasks (§5), and supplies a training signal unavailable in SFT-only. They trained over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks. Summary bullets: same-data ICL/SFT do not align in activation space (§3); IA2 enforces ICL functional alignment and drastically improves SFT; IA2 signal is not present in SFT-only (§5). Figure 1 says standard SFT enforces only output-space alignment and causes subpar performance/miscalibration in low-data; IA2 activation matching boosts adaptation quality.

Title/claim: IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) improves SFT by self-distilling/replicating ICL activation patterns in SFT models before normal SFT. Abstract/intro: ICL and SFT can give similar token outputs but distinct activations (§3); ICL generalizes/calibrates well in few-shot but has inference/context cost. IA2 uses same data as SFT: collect ICL activations, enforce functional/activation alignment, then SFT. Claimed significant/drastic gains in accuracy and calibration on 12 benchmarks, two model families; >13,000 models. IA2 signal claimed unavailable in SFT-only.

§2 definitions/notation: Decoder-only transformer LM M_Θ; self-attention output SA(T;W_QKVO)=Z with z_i=softmax(q_i K^T/sqrt(d)) V W_O, q_i=t_i W_Q, K=t_:i W_K, V=t_:i W_V; Z same shape R×d as input T. They study behavior changes from context T or weights W_QKVO. SFT: dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}_{i=1}^N; fine-tune Θ→Θ′ so M_Θ′(X_t)=first response token ybar_t, repeated for full response. If Y_i has G tokens, generate G tokens Ybar_i and minimize cross-entropy sum over generated/ground-truth tokens: L_SFT=sum_i sum_j CE(Ybar_ij,Y_ij). ICL: prompt frozen M_Θ with demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] plus test X_t; output M_Θ(I∘X_t)=ŷ_t without weight updates; classic demo-pair setting. Activations: hidden SA outputs, tensor A size L×R×d for L layers/R tokens. They study T=[I∘X] for ICL and T=X without ICL under different weights. Activation similarity asim(A1,A2): token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors, size L×R.

Title/claim: IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) improves SFT by self-distilling/replicating ICL activation patterns in SFT models before normal SFT. Abstract/intro: ICL and SFT can give similar token outputs but distinct activations (§3); ICL generalizes/calibrates well in few-shot but has inference/context cost. IA2 uses same data as SFT: collect ICL activations, enforce functional/activation alignment, then SFT. Claimed significant/drastic gains in accuracy and calibration on 12 benchmarks, two model families; >13,000 models; IA2 signal unavailable in SFT-only.

§2 definitions: SFT dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}; fine-tune Θ→Θ′ on cross-entropy over response tokens. ICL: frozen model prompted with demos I=[X1Y1…XnYn] plus test X_t. Activations are self-attention outputs, tensor A size L×R×d. asim(A1,A2): token-wise cosine similarity, size L×R.

§3: Tests whether ICL and SFT are practically/functionally equivalent. Collected A_ICL with T=[I∘X] for 100 test samples from datasets including SST2/AGNews on Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 families (1B/16 layers, 3B/28, 4B/36). Trained SFT models using same ICL demos until convergence; collected A_SFT with T=X. Calculated asim(A_ICL,A_SFT) at output token positions, averaged across tokens/samples/datasets. Claim: ICL and SFT activations are not aligned; alignment better in initial/final layers, worse in middle. Figure 2 also claims IA2→SFT aligns much more with ICL than SFT-only and performs better. §3 claims Figure 1 shows ICL much more calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy; motivation: use information-rich ICL activations to improve SFT.
