Title/claim: IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) improves SFT by self-distilling/replicating ICL activation patterns before normal SFT, using same data as SFT. Abstract/intro: ICL and SFT can give similar token outputs but distinct activations (§3); ICL has better few-shot generalization/calibration but inference/context cost. Claimed significant/drastic gains in accuracy/calibration on 12 benchmarks, two model families, >13,000 models.

§2: SFT dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}; fine-tune Θ→Θ′ with cross-entropy on response tokens. ICL: frozen model prompted with demos I=[X1Y1…XnYn]+test X_t. Activations are self-attention outputs A size L×R×d. asim(A1,A2): token-wise cosine similarity, size L×R.

§3: Collected A_ICL with T=[I∘X] for 100 test samples from datasets incl. SST2/AGNews on Qwen3/Llama-3.2 families (1B/16 layers, 3B/28, 4B/36). SFT models trained using same ICL demos until convergence; A_SFT with T=X. asim at output token positions averaged across tokens/samples/datasets. Claim: ICL/SFT activations poorly aligned, especially middle layers; initial/final better. Fig 1: ICL much more calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy. Fig 2: IA2→SFT aligns more with ICL than SFT-only and performs better.

§4: IA2 goal: for each layer find modified attention weights so SA([I∘X];W_QKVO)≈SA(X;~W_QKVO) for newly generated token index -1. Procedure: generate ICL responses Ŷ_i with T_i=[I∘X_i], using remaining samples to construct I; collect A_ICL^i ∈ R^{L×G×d} at output positions. Then feed [X_i∘Ŷ_i] without demos to get A^i; train model parameters to align A^i to A_ICL^i. Text calls this MSE but Eq(4) is sum of norms. Then continue standard SFT with ground-truth Y until convergence.

§5 setup: Experiments in single-token and multi-token settings. Single-token: Sentiment uses SST2, Financial Phrasebank (FinS), Poem Sentiment (PoemS); train on SST2 and FinS and evaluate on all three, described as one ID + 2 OOD per training set. True/False: StrategyQA (STF). News: train AGNews (AGN), eval AGN and BBCNews (BBCN). MCQ: SciQ and QASC with answer choices remapped to unrelated token set, named SciQr/QASCr; train SciQr, eval both. Multi-token: train GSM8K, eval GSM8K and GSM Symbolic (GSM8Ks); HMath Algebra (HMathA); SciQ free-form answer generation.

Data scarce setup: for each task create training sets with N in powers of 2 [2,4,8,16,...], 5 random sets per N. For IA2 activations A_ICL^i, use remaining N-1 training samples as ICL demos in random order for each Xi, reusing same training data for fairness. Evaluation uses separate 500-sample set per task. Appendix A has dataset processing.

Multi-token outputs are standard text chain-of-thought style (not <think> tags) followed by answer in demo-specified format. GSM8K/GSM8Ks ground truth format: reasoning #### numerical answer; accuracy by parsing numerical answer, exact match, with additional parsing variants like “The answer is <value>”. Title IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves SFT. Q7M/SFT label-trained; V2K/ICL demos no updates. IA2/R8D: generate Ŷ using demos, collect V2K output activations, feed query-only [X∘Ŷ], optimize activation alignment, then train target responses with Q7M. Metrics: U6R accuracy, D8P ECE; multi-token correctness only. Methods: H9C=SFT only, J3N=IA2 only, P4Z=IA2→SFT; T6B=simultaneous IA2+SFT; F5W=SFT soft labels/KD comparator.

Earlier Qwen3-4B N=4: Table1 single-token P4Z usually best but W3F→Y8J H9C 31.8 > P4Z 27.9; N5Q P4Z 62.4 < V2K 66.0, conflicting with any “across board” caption. Table2 multi-token: P4Z > H9C all rows, sometimes < V2K/J3N. A5Y subspace overlap definition recorded.

Part10 Table6 IA3 on Llama-3.2 N=4: P4Z U6R > H9C and V2K in all 5 rows; P4Z D8P not always best and sometimes worse than V2K/H9C/J3N.

Part11 Related Work claims present experiments find Q7M worse; conflicts with P4Z>SFT-based Q7M pipeline outperforming V2K in Table6 U6R. Conclusion claims V2K often richer/generalizable and R8D moves to adaptable subspace; no new clear contradiction.

Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Abstract claims: SFT trains weights for target responses; ICL adapts at inference via prompt instructions/demonstrations. ICL can have better generalizability and calibration than SFT in data-scarce settings but higher inference compute. Authors claim they show ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns, implying different functional mechanisms. They introduce ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation technique to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. IA2 is performed as a priming step before SFT and is claimed to significantly improve accuracy and calibration across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families. Need check later for consistency with: 12 benchmarks, two model families, IA2 as priming before SFT, improvements in both accuracy and calibration, and claims about distinct activation patterns.

Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Abstract/introduction claims: SFT adapts weights to labeled samples; ICL adapts at inference via prompt demonstrations/instructions. ICL generalizes well in few-shot and is well calibrated, but costs context/inference compute. SFT can overfit/shortcut in few-shot and be miscalibrated/subpar. Authors claim ICL and SFT with same data can look similar in token/output space but produce disparate internal activations, indicating different functional mechanisms (§3). Hypothesis: ICL activations contain rich information about extracting generalizable patterns from context, absent in few-shot SFT.

IA2 = ICL Activation Alignment, a self-distillation/priming method: (1) collect information-rich ICL activations, (2) enforce functional alignment with ICL by matching activations, then (3) perform SFT on the primed model using same data. Claimed to improve SFT performance/quality and calibration across text classification and generation tasks. Abstract says across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families; intro says trained over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks. Need check later for two model families and calibration results.

Contributions to verify later: (1) ICL and SFT with same data do not align in activation space; (2) IA2 priming before SFT drastically improves performance; (3) IA2 training signal is not present in SFT-only training and is important. Figure 1 described as showing standard SFT enforces output-space alignment only and IA2 matches rich ICL activation patterns; comparison charts aggregated across models/datasets in §5.

SFT dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}_{i=1}^N; weights Θ→Θ′; for response Y_i of G tokens, loss L_SFT=sum_i sum_j CE(̄Y_ij,Y_ij). ICL prompts original M_Θ with demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘...∘X_n∘Y_n] plus test X_t, no weight updates, output M_Θ(I∘X_t)=ŷ_t; paper focuses on classic input-output demo ICL. Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Key terms: Q7M=SFT/weight adaptation; V2K=ICL demos; K4X=token-wise cosine activation similarity; R8D/IA2 aligns layerwise SA activations at generated token positions; P4Z=R8D then Q7M; J3N=R8D-only; H9C=Q7M/SFT; A5Y=subspace overlap=(1/r)||U1^T U2||_F^2, r=8. Earlier issue: prose says MSE but formula sum of norms.

Setup: LoRA rank 8 on WQ/WK/WO, >13k models; train to convergence up to 50 epochs; LR {1e-4,3e-4,1e-3}; Qwen3-4B all tasks; Llama variants secondary. Multi-token no calibration, gen limits 200/400. V2K demos eval 5 times; trained methods no demos.

Internal errors found: (1) Table 1 caption claimed P4Z beats Q7M/H9C across board, but W3F→Y8J H9C 31.8 > P4Z 27.9. (2) Text after Table 4 says F5W soft-label SFT significantly worse than standard Q7M in multi-token, but Table 4 L9S F5W 36.1 > H9C/Q7M 28.2 and caption says baseline improves on Q7M.

Table 3 trains on V2K responses: T6B generally > H9C; H9C/P4Z worse than ground-truth training. Table 5 Qwen math shot evolution: V2K exceeds all training methods on L9S/V7B; P4Z gap to V2K shrinks with shots and remains >H9C. Table 6 Llama-3.2 N=4 with (IA)3: P4Z U6R > H9C and > V2K in all 5 rows. Conclusion says V2K often richer/generalizable and R8D shifts into more adaptable subspace; no new inconsistency.

Authors claim they show ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns, implying different functional mechanisms. They introduce ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation technique to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. IA2 is performed as a priming step before SFT and is claimed to significantly improve accuracy and calibration across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families. Need check later for consistency with: 12 benchmarks, two model families, IA2 as priming before SFT, improvements in both accuracy and calibration, and claims about distinct activation patterns.

Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Abstract/introduction claims: SFT adapts weights to labeled samples; ICL adapts at inference via prompt demonstrations/instructions. ICL generalizes well in few-shot and is well calibrated, but costs context/inference compute. SFT can overfit/shortcut in few-shot and be miscalibrated/subpar. Authors claim ICL and SFT with same data can look similar in token/output space but produce disparate internal activations, indicating different functional mechanisms (§3). Hypothesis: ICL activations contain rich information about extracting generalizable patterns from context, absent in few-shot SFT.

IA2 = ICL Activation Alignment, a self-distillation/priming method: (1) collect information-rich ICL activations, (2) enforce functional alignment with ICL by matching activations, then (3) perform SFT on the primed model using same data. Claimed to improve SFT performance/quality and calibration across text classification and generation tasks. Abstract says across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families; intro says trained over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks. Need check later for two model families and calibration results.

Contributions to verify later: (1) ICL and SFT with same data do not align in activation space; (2) IA2 priming before SFT drastically improves performance; (3) IA2 training signal is not present in SFT-only training and is important. Intro framing/definitions to track: Q7M appears to mean weight adaptation/fine-tuning/PEFT; V2K appears to mean in-context demonstrations/instructions. Q7M needs many labeled samples; V2K consumes context capacity and per-query inference compute. Research question: whether information-rich V2K activations can improve Q7M quality. Hypothesis: V2K activations encode generalizable contextual patterns absent from few-shot weight adaptation, which may take shortcuts/overfit target responses. Similar token-space behavior may mask different internal processing.

Intro says context-to-weight distillation using response-text/output signals can inherit output-training problems because matching context-conditioned outputs does not ensure matching functioning. Figure 1 claims standard Q7M enforces output-space agreement between response and target—the third step of proposed pipeline—and gives subpar performance/miscalibration under low data. Proposed pipeline: collect rich V2K activations, enforce functional alignment, then train against target responses. Figure 1 comparison charts aggregate performance across models/datasets, details §5. Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Authors Aayush Mishra, Daniel Khashabi, Anqi Liu. Abstract claims: Across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, P4Z significantly improves output U6R and calibration; R8D self-distills by replicating V2K activation patterns in weight-trained models, incentivizing V2K-like internal reasoning; priming signal unavailable through H9C.

Key terms/definitions: Q7M = supervised fine-tuning/weight adaptation/SFT; V2K = in-context learning/ICL with demonstrations; K4X = activation similarity/asim, token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors, shape L×R. For task data D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}. Q7M changes weights Θ→Θ′ and minimizes cross-entropy across G response tokens (Eq. 2). V2K uses concatenated demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘...∘Xn∘Yn], predicts M_Θ(I∘X_t) without weight updates; present setting restricts demonstrations to classic input-output pairs, though ICL can include generic instructions.

Transformer notation: decoder-only LM stacks self-attention and linear layers. SA formula Eq. 1 with W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O; K,V use t_:i (causal first i tokens). Activations are hidden SA outputs, A∈R^{L×R×d}. Studied sequences for activation comparison are T=[I∘X] with demonstrations and T=X without demonstrations under differing weights.

Intro claims to check later: Q7M needs many labeled samples; V2K uses context/inference compute. Hypothesis: V2K activations encode generalizable contextual patterns absent from few-shot weight adaptation, whose similar outputs may mask different internal processing. Title: IA2 aligns SFT activations with ICL, improving performance/calibration. §2 asim token-wise cosine. §3: SFT/no-demo activations differ from ICL/base; ICL better calibrated at similar/slightly better acc; IA2→SFT more aligned and better. §4 IA2: generate ICL response using other samples as demos; match no-demo activations on [Xi∘Ŷi] by MSE, then SFT on ground truth.

§5 tasks: Qwen3-4B all tasks; Llama secondary. LoRA rank 8 WQ/WK/WO; N up to 16 Llama, 8 Qwen. Table1 Qwen N=4 single-token caption says IA2→SFT outperforms SFT across board, but exceptions: BBC acc, SST ECE tie, PoemS/STF ECE worse. Table2 Qwen N=4 multi-token: IA2→SFT beats SFT all; IA2 only best GSM8K 77.4; ICL best HMathA 60.4.

§5.2: more activation similarity improves ECE; extreme ICL alignment may hurt acc. LoRA subspace: SFT nearly orthogonal to IA2/IA2→SFT; IA2→SFT shares ~39% avg subspace with IA2.

§6: simultaneous IA2+SFT hard due response-length mismatch; self-distills on ICL responses. Table3 Qwen N=4 on ICL responses: IA2+SFT > SFT only. Table4 KD Llama: GSM8K soft labels 36.1 vs SFT 28.2, near IA2+SFT 37.0; SST2 soft labels 55.9 below IA2-based.

Table5 Qwen math shots. GSM8K: ICL 81.2/76.4/77.2 for N=2/4/8; IA2→SFT 74.6/73.6/76.0; IA2 only beats ICL at N=4,8. HMathA ICL 58.6/60.4/62.1 beats all; IA2→SFT gap closes. Table6 Llama (IA)3 N=4: IA2→SFT acc exceeds SFT and ICL in all shown cases, but ECE sometimes worse.

Conclusion claims IA2 consistently improves SFT accuracy/calibration, conflicting with exceptions above. Future work: diversity, catastrophic forgetting, RL-tuned models. Reproducibility statement says code on GitHub and §5/appendix/README with fixed seeds should reproduce results.

final_notes:
Title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Q7M=SFT/weight adaptation; V2K=ICL demos; K4X=token-wise cosine activation similarity. R8D/IA2 aligns layerwise SA activations at generated-token positions. Possible internal issue: prose says MSE but formula sum of norms.

Setup: train each method/dataset to convergence up to 50 epochs, LR {1e-4,3e-4,1e-3}, best selected; >13k models. Rank-8 LoRA on WQ, WK, WO. Multi-token N limited: Llama 16, Qwen 8. Activation cap G=200; target-token training uses ground-truth response length. Single-token metrics U6R=accuracy, D8P=ECE; V2K demos eval 5 times, trained methods no demos. Multi-token only correctness.

Models: Qwen3-4B-Base all tasks; Llama-3.2-1B except E2T uses 3B for single-token; multi-token secondary Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct.

Reported internal issue from part 7: Table 1 Qwen N=4 single-token caption claims P4Z outperforms H9C/Q7M across board, but W3F→Y8J has H9C U6R 31.8 > P4Z 27.9. Table 2 Qwen N=4 multi-token: P4Z exceeds H9C all rows but underperforms V2K on L9S and V7B. Fig.3: D8P decreases with K4X; extreme alignment can leave U6R gains.

Part 9: Table3 Qwen N=4 multi-token training on V2K responses: T6B usually best except V7B P4Z 54.0 > T6B 53.6. Table4 KD/soft-label comparison: L9S Llama-Instruct, B7V Llama-1B. Table5 Qwen math shots: P4Z gap to V2K closes from N=2 to 8; L9S V2K N=2 81.2 > N=4/8.

Part 10: Table6 Llama-3.2 N=4 with (IA)3 instead of LoRA. P4Z U6R exceeds H9C and V2K in all listed rows; D8P often worse than V2K/H9C.

Conclusion: V2K often richer/more generalizable; R8D shifts models to adaptable subspace; future work diversity/forgetting/RL-tuned models. Reproducibility says GitHub plus appendix/README/seeds suffice.

Transformer notation: decoder-only LM stacks self-attention and linear layers. SA formula Eq. 1 with W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O; K,V use t_:i (causal first i tokens). Activations are hidden SA outputs, A∈R^{L×R×d}. Studied sequences for activation comparison are T=[I∘X] with demonstrations and T=X without demonstrations under differing weights.

They introduce ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation technique to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Abstract/introduction claims: SFT adapts weights to labeled samples; ICL adapts at inference via prompt demonstrations/instructions. ICL generalizes well in few-shot and is well calibrated, but costs context/inference compute. SFT can overfit/shortcut in few-shot and be miscalibrated/subpar. Authors claim ICL and SFT with same data can look similar in token/output space but produce disparate internal activations, indicating different functional mechanisms (§3). Hypothesis: ICL activations contain rich information about extracting generalizable patterns from context, absent in few-shot SFT.

IA2 = ICL Activation Alignment, a self-distillation/priming method: (1) collect information-rich ICL activations, (2) enforce functional alignment with ICL by matching activations, then (3) perform SFT on the primed model using same data. Claimed to improve SFT performance/quality and calibration across text classification and generation tasks. Abstract says across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families; intro says trained over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks. Need check later for two model families and calibration results.

Contributions to verify later: (1) ICL and SFT with same data do not align in activation space; (2) IA2 priming before SFT drastically improves performance; (3) IA2 training signal is not present in SFT-only training and is important. Figure 1 described as showing standard SFT enforces output-space alignment only and IA2 matches rich ICL activation patterns; comparison charts aggregated across models/datasets in §5.

§2 definitions: Decoder-only transformer LM M_Θ; self-attention uses W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O (W_QKVO). SA output per token z_i = softmax(q_i K^T/sqrt(d)) V · W_O, with q_i=t_i W_Q, K=t_:i W_K, V=t_:i W_V; Z same shape R×d as T. SFT dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}_{i=1}^N; weights Θ→Θ′; for response Y_i of G tokens, loss L_SFT=sum_i sum_j CE(̄Y_ij,Y_ij). ICL prompts original M_Θ with demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘...∘X_n∘Y_n] plus test X_t, no weight updates, output M_Θ(I∘X_t)=ŷ_t; paper focuses on classic input-output demo ICL. Activations = hidden SA outputs. For L layers and R tokens, activation tensor A size L×R×d. They study T=[I∘X] for ICL and T=X without ICL under different weights. Activation similarity asim(A1,A2)=token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors, size L×R (requires comparable token dimensions).

Hypothesis: ICL activations encode generalizable pattern extraction absent in few-shot SFT. IA2 = collect ICL activations, align model activations to them, then SFT on same data; claimed to improve SFT quality/performance and calibration across text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, two model families; intro says >13,000 models.

§2 definitions: Decoder-only LM M_Θ; self-attention W_Q,K,V,O and output z_i = softmax(q_i K^T/sqrt(d)) V · W_O. SFT dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)}; loss over response tokens. ICL prompt uses demos I=[X1∘Y1...X_n∘Y_n]+test X_t, no weight update. Activations = hidden SA outputs; activation tensor A is L×R×d. final_notes:
Title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves SFT.” Terms: Q7M=SFT/weight adaptation; V2K=ICL demos; K4X=activation cosine/asim; A5Y=subspace overlap=(1/r)||U1^T U2||_F^2. Models: Qwen3, Llama-3.2; 1B=16 layers, 3B=28, 4B=36. R8D/IA2 aligns layerwise processing, not output similarity; prose says MSE but formula sums norms.

Sec5: rank-8 LoRA on WQ/WK/WO, up to 50 epochs, >13k models. Sec5.1 claimed P4Z beats H9C almost all and mostly exceeds V2K, but Table1 had exceptions; also claimed J3N >95% E2T though Table1 E2T J3N 90.4, P4Z 91.7. Table2 multi: P4Z > H9C all rows but sometimes < V2K. Sec5.2/Fig3: D8P decreases as K4X to V2K increases; P4Z intermediate. H9C updates orthogonal; P4Z shares J3N space; best P4Z/J3N overlap ~39%.

Sec6: T6B=IA2+SFT on V2K/self-distilled responses using L_R8D + beta L_Q7M; beta spans J3N to H9C. Table3 Qwen3-4B N=4: T6B > H9C on L9S/X4C/V7B/O3D. Table4 KD/F5W: L9S multi F5W 36.1 vs H9C 28.2, T6B 37.0; B7V single F5W 55.9 vs T6B 66.9. Table5: P4Z gap to V2K shrinks; L9S N=4,8 J3N > V2K.

Part10: IA3 Table6 Llama-3.2 N=4: P4Z U6R exceeds H9C and V2K all 5 rows; D8P not always better.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 sets up classical surrogate risk minimization. Data (X_i,Y_i) iid P; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk Eq. (1): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)]. Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn, loss 1{yy'≤0}, risk P(Yf(X)≤0). They then generalize task risk to depend on conditional distribution: Eq. (2) R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]; in multiclass, ell(yhat,P)=sum_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} recovers 0-1 error. Surrogate loss phi:R^d×Y→R; surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/all Borel F and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified F; message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z∈Z, e.g. m noisy labels Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m). Aggregation space A, aggregator A:Z→A, surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+. Aggregated surrogate risk Eq. (3): R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], asking when minimizing it suffices for task risk Eq. (2).

Example 1 repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Example 2 KNN abstraction: X has label Y and additional iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m; order by distance, X_(0)=X. For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will handle single-sample aggregation.

Section 3 assumes F all Borel f:X→R^d for standard surrogate consistency. Conditional risks: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s. Consistency notions: (i) Fisher: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi>0 on eps>0 with psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi*. Calibration psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi=inf_x. Cor 3.1: Fisher iff psi(eps,x)>0 all x, eps>0; Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi gives comparison if overline positive.

They argue for general risk (2), single-label surrogate consistency is generally impossible, motivating aggregation theory Sec 3.2.

Sec 3.1 ranking example: Y={(i,j):i≠j,1≤i,j≤k}, (i,j)=i ranked above j. For conditional p_ij, define C_x with diag 0, offdiag (C_x)_ij=p_ij/sum_{l≠j}p_lj, 0/0=1/(k-1), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank items by C_x 1. Task loss ell(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(e_i-e_j)^T C1≤0 and (e_i-e_j)^T C1≠0}; task risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (Eq 4). Restrict scores to sum zero. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex-in-score surrogate phi:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for Eq 4.

With aggregation, collect m iid comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)|X, m≥k. Define counts m_ij (intended comparison counts) and m_j=sum_i m_ij; A(Z)=star if any m_j=0, otherwise vector_i sum_j m_ij/m_j. Regressing on A(Z) when not star yields consistency (Prop 2 follows).

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures using aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses have robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g. zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Main theme: cleaning/refining noisy label signals improves robustness across data collection, model fitting, and prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract/main intro claims: label cleaning/aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness faces: (1) improved estimation consistency: with surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can yield consistent optimal prediction when impossible without aggregation/raw (X,Y) pairs; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can give consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Intro motivates asking whether aggregation is needed and how it helps. Claimed contributions/examples: ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where estimators using only pairs (X,Y) necessarily fail, but aggregation yields consistency. Develop new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation. In fully nonparametric settings, show number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. Aggregation lets them prove surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions on surrogate loss; losses using aggregated labels admit approximate linear comparison inequalities. Unlike conventional risk consistency theory requiring all measurable functions as hypothesis class F, they will show classification results where aggregation guarantees consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes, which may fail without aggregation.

Title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Main claims from intro: label aggregation/cleaning can provide robustness impossible without aggregation: improved surrogate consistency and finite-dimensional consistency under misspecification. Examples promised include ranking/binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where raw-pair estimators fail but aggregation succeeds; new theory for surrogate consistency with aggregation; approximate linear comparison inequalities; restricted hypothesis classes can become consistent with aggregation.

Section 2 preliminaries: Data (X,Y) iid from P, scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk first defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary example d(s)=sgn(s), ell=1{yy'≤0}, R=P(Yf(X)≤0). Then generalized task risk depends on conditional distribution: R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(.|X))] (eq 2); multiclass example ell(ŷ,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{ŷ≠y}, equals standard 0-1 error. Surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) classical Fisher consistency with all Borel functions and (ii) parametric/misspecified F. Message: aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z; repeated labels example Z=(Y1,…,Ym). Aggregation A:Z→Aspace (e.g. majority vote), surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), ask when minimizing it suffices for task risk (2). Example 1: A is empirical minimizer of Σ_l ell(y,Y_l); with 0-1 loss this is majority vote. Example 2: KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(Xi,Yi)_{i=1}^m), order neighbors by distance to X, set X_(0)=X, aggregate A_{m,K}=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)); Appendix C treats single-sample version.

Section 3 standard surrogate consistency for all Borel F. Conditional risks: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)); R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Excess deltas; R*=inf_F R, R_phi*=inf_F R_phi. Consistency notions: (i) Fisher: R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R* for all P; (ii) uniform comparison psi(R-R*)≤R_phi-R_phi*, psi positive on eps>0. Calibration psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x):delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi=inf_x. Cor 3.1: Fisher iff psi(eps,x)>0 all x,eps; Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi gives comparison if positive.

They say generally impossible to get Fisher-consistent surrogate using only paired (X,Y), motivating aggregation.

Sec 3.1 ranking: Y={(i,j):i≠j} pairwise comparisons, p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define C_x with diagonal 0, offdiag p_ij/sum_{l≠j}p_lj, 0/0=1/(k-1); C_x^T 1=1. Rank by C_x 1. Loss ell(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(e_i-e_j)^T C1≤0 and (e_i-e_j)^T C1≠0}; task risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (eq4). Scores restricted to sum zero. Proposition 1: for k≥3, any convex phi:R^k×Y→R is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk.

Aggregation for ranking: collect m independent comparisons Z=(Y1,...,Ym), claim consistency when m≥k. Define counts m_ij and m_j (formula in text seems oddly written); A(Z)=star if any m_j=0, else vector_i Σ_j m_ij/m_j. Regressing on A(Z) when not star yields consistency; Proposition 2 follows but statement not yet shown.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

errors.evidence: The paper first defines the original task risk as Eq. (1): “the goal is to minimize the task risk … R(f):=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)].” It then introduces Eq. (2) as the “slightly more sophisticated version” depending on P(Y∈·|X).
errors.explanation: Calling Eq. (2) the “original problem” is inconsistent with the immediately preceding setup: Eq. (1), not Eq. (2), is the original instantaneous-label task-risk problem. Eq. (2) cannot be both the new version and the original problem it is said to coincide with.

steps.notes_before:
Section 2 sets up classical surrogate risk minimization. Data (X_i,Y_i) iid P; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk Eq. (1): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)]. Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn, loss 1{yy'≤0}, risk P(Yf(X)≤0). They then generalize task risk to depend on conditional distribution: Eq. (2) R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]; in multiclass, ell(yhat,P)=sum_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} recovers 0-1 error. Surrogate loss phi:R^d×Y→R; surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/all Borel F and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified F; message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z∈Z, e.g. m noisy labels Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m). Aggregation space A, aggregator A:Z→A, surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+. Aggregated surrogate risk Eq. (3): R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], asking when minimizing it suffices for task risk Eq. (2).

Example 1 repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Example 2 KNN abstraction: X has label Y and additional iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m; order by distance, X_(0)=X. For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will handle single-sample aggregation.

Section 3 assumes F all Borel f:X→R^d for standard surrogate consistency. Conditional risks: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s. Consistency notions: (i) Fisher: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi>0 on eps>0 with psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi*. Calibration psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi=inf_x. Cor 3.1: Fisher iff psi(eps,x)>0 all x, eps>0; Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi gives comparison if overline positive.

They argue for general risk (2), single-label surrogate consistency is generally impossible, motivating aggregation theory Sec 3.2.

Sec 3.1 ranking example: Y={(i,j):i≠j,1≤i,j≤k}, (i,j)=i ranked above j. For conditional p_ij, define C_x with diag 0, offdiag (C_x)_ij=p_ij/sum_{l≠j}p_lj, 0/0=1/(k-1), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank items by C_x 1. Task loss ell(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(e_i-e_j)^T C1≤0 and (e_i-e_j)^T C1≠0}; task risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (Eq 4). Restrict scores to sum zero. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex-in-score surrogate phi:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for Eq 4.

With aggregation, collect m iid comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)|X, m≥k. Define counts m_ij (intended comparison counts) and m_j=sum_i m_ij; A(Z)=star if any m_j=0, otherwise vector_i sum_j m_ij/m_j. Regressing on A(Z) when not star yields consistency (Prop 2 follows).

errors.evidence: The same sentence says it is defining “the pointwise and uniform calibration functions,” and earlier notes record the standard uniform calibration function as “overline psi=inf_x.” Also \overline{\psi}_{A}(\epsilon,x) has no dependence on s, while x remains free in the displayed definition.
errors.explanation: The claimed uniform calibration function is internally inconsistent with both the stated pointwise/uniform distinction and the earlier definition: it should take an infimum over x, not over s.

steps.notes_before:
End Sec 3.1/Prop 2: define phi(s,q)=||s-q||^2, phi(s,star)=0. If m≥k, phi is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4). Reason Prop1 fails but Prop2 succeeds: aggregation expands response space from Y to R^k.

Sec 3.2: aggregation and consistency. For arbitrary A:Z→A, conditional surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(s|x)=E[phi(s,A(Z))|X=x], excess delta_{phi,A}. Eq (5) defines pointwise calibration overline psi_A(eps,x)=inf_s{delta_{phi,A}(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; displayed uniform definition incorrectly says inf_s overline psi_A(eps,x) though should be inf_x. Prop3: assuming integrable b with delta_ell(f(x),x)≤b(x), phi Fisher consistent for task risk (2) iff overline psi_A(eps,x)>0 all x, eps>0; Fenchel biconjugate psi_A yields comparison psi_A(R(f)-R*)≤R_{phi,A}(f)-R_{phi,A}*.

Sec 3.2.2: finite label space |Y|=k (note footnote: in ranking example earlier k was ranking length and |Y|=k(k-1); henceforth k means label-space cardinality). Identifying surrogate Def 3.1: phi:R^d×A→R is (C1,C2)-identifying if exist a_y∈A, s_y∈R^d with d(s_y)=y and for y≠y’: (6a) phi(s_y,a_y)+C1 ≤ inf_{d∘s≠y} phi(s,a_y); (6b) phi(s_y,a_y’)-C2 ≤ inf_s phi(s,a_y’). No convexity or nonaggregated consistency required. Example: binary hinge with A=Y={±1}, a_y=s_y=y is (1,2)-identifying. Generalized majority aggregation A_m(y_1..y_m)=a_hat_y where hat_y=argmin_y sum_i ell(y,y_i), ties arbitrary. Cor 3.2: if m(n)→∞ and phi identifying, surrogate excess for A_m→0 implies task excess→0.

final_notes:
Earlier key points: Section 3 defines surrogate calibration/Q7D comparison ψ(R−R*)≤surrogate excess. Ranking Prop1 says no convex Q7D for k≥3; Prop2 squared loss with aggregation Q7D. Theorem1 W3C+A_m+Nα: if excess ≥ξ(M)=2P(κ>M)+(4C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1−α)}, task excess ≤16/Cφ1 aggregated surrogate excess. Noted possible internal issues: α=1 discussion despite formula division by zero; Nα/Mβ gives α=1/2→β=1 but text says 2; Lemma3.2 coefficient 16N and Lemma3.3 coefficient 8/min loss may conflict with Theorem1’s 16/Cφ1.

Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

(2) R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]; in multiclass, ell(yhat,P)=sum_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} recovers 0-1 error. Surrogate loss phi:R^d×Y→R; surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/all Borel F and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified F; message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z∈Z, e.g. m noisy labels Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m). Aggregation space A, aggregator A:Z→A, surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+. Aggregated surrogate risk Eq. (3): R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], asking when minimizing it suffices for task risk Eq. (2).

Example 1 repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 sets up classical surrogate risk minimization. Data (X_i,Y_i) iid P; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk Eq. (1): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)]. Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn, loss 1{yy'≤0}, risk P(Yf(X)≤0). They then generalize task risk to depend on conditional distribution: Eq. (2) R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]; in multiclass, ell(yhat,P)=sum_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} recovers 0-1 error. Surrogate loss phi:R^d×Y→R; surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/all Borel F and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified F; message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z∈Z, e.g. m noisy labels Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m). Aggregation space A, aggregator A:Z→A, surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+. Aggregated surrogate risk Eq. (3): R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], asking when minimizing it suffices for task risk Eq. (2).

Example 1 repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Example 2 KNN abstraction: X has label Y and additional iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m; order by distance, X_(0)=X. For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will handle single-sample aggregation.

Section 3 assumes F all Borel f:X→R^d for standard surrogate consistency. Conditional risks: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s. Consistency notions: (i) Fisher: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi>0 on eps>0 with psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi*. Calibration psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi=inf_x. Cor 3.1: Fisher iff psi(eps,x)>0 all x, eps>0; Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi gives comparison if overline positive.

They argue for general risk (2), single-label surrogate consistency is generally impossible, motivating aggregation theory Sec 3.2.

Sec 3.1 ranking example: Y={(i,j):i≠j,1≤i,j≤k}, (i,j)=i ranked above j. For conditional p_ij, define C_x with diag 0, offdiag (C_x)_ij=p_ij/sum_{l≠j}p_lj, 0/0=1/(k-1), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank items by C_x 1. Task loss ell(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(e_i-e_j)^T C1≤0 and (e_i-e_j)^T C1≠0}; task risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (Eq 4). Restrict scores to sum zero. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex-in-score surrogate phi:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for Eq 4.

With aggregation, collect m iid comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)|X, m≥k. Define counts m_ij (intended comparison counts) and m_j=sum_i m_ij; A(Z)=star if any m_j=0, otherwise vector_i sum_j m_ij/m_j. Regressing on A(Z) when not star yields consistency (Prop 2 follows).

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning procedures using aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses have robustness properties impossible without cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses vs task losses, label aggregation gives stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may favor using all information/modeling label uncertainty for efficiency, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers with every fixed label count. Overall theme: refining noisy signals via aggregation/cleaning improves robustness across collection, fitting, and prediction.

Title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract: cleaned/aggregated labels give robustness impossible without cleaning; stronger surrogate-to-task consistency than raw labels; even if perfectly specified models might favor all noisy info for efficiency, consistency can fail for standard methods under slight misspecification; aggregation converges to optimal classifiers with fixed label count.

Intro claims: Data collection often involves multiple noisy/crowdsourced labels and denoising to gold labels. Paper studies how aggregation improves consistency. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved estimation consistency—surrogate loss minimization (e.g. multiclass logistic) can be task-consistent (e.g. zero-one) with aggregated labels even when impossible without aggregation; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivating questions: whether aggregation is needed/helpful for consistency. They promise concrete examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where using only pairs (X,Y) necessarily fails, but label aggregation is consistent. They develop new theory for surrogate consistency with aggregation. In fully nonparametric scenarios, number of aggregated samples combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. Aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate-loss conditions. Unlike conventional risk consistency requiring all measurable functions, aggregation can guarantee consistency over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.
