Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 sets up classical surrogate risk minimization. Data (X_i,Y_i) iid P; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk Eq. (1): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)]. Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn, loss 1{yy'≤0}, risk P(Yf(X)≤0). They then generalize task risk to depend on conditional distribution: Eq. (2) R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]; in multiclass, ell(yhat,P)=sum_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} recovers 0-1 error. Surrogate loss phi:R^d×Y→R; surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/all Borel F and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified F; message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z∈Z, e.g. m noisy labels Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m). Aggregation space A, aggregator A:Z→A, surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+. Aggregated surrogate risk Eq. (3): R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], asking when minimizing it suffices for task risk Eq. (2).

Example 1 repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Example 2 KNN abstraction: X has label Y and additional iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m; order by distance, X_(0)=X. For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will handle single-sample aggregation.

Section 3 assumes F all Borel f:X→R^d for standard surrogate consistency. Conditional risks: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s. Consistency notions: (i) Fisher: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi>0 on eps>0 with psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi*. Calibration psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi=inf_x. Cor 3.1: Fisher iff psi(eps,x)>0 all x, eps>0; Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi gives comparison if overline positive.

They argue for general risk (2), single-label surrogate consistency is generally impossible, motivating aggregation theory Sec 3.2.

Sec 3.1 ranking example: Y={(i,j):i≠j,1≤i,j≤k}, (i,j)=i ranked above j. For conditional p_ij, define C_x with diag 0, offdiag (C_x)_ij=p_ij/sum_{l≠j}p_lj, 0/0=1/(k-1), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank items by C_x 1. Task loss ell(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i-s_j)(e_i-e_j)^T C1≤0 and (e_i-e_j)^T C1≠0}; task risk R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X1 order differently) (Eq 4). Restrict scores to sum zero. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex-in-score surrogate phi:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for Eq 4.

With aggregation, collect m iid comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)|X, m≥k. Define counts m_ij (intended comparison counts) and m_j=sum_i m_ij; A(Z)=star if any m_j=0, otherwise vector_i sum_j m_ij/m_j. Regressing on A(Z) when not star yields consistency (Prop 2 follows).

errors.claim: “\overline{\psi}_{A}(\epsilon)\coloneqq\inf_{s\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\overline{\psi}_{A}(\epsilon,x)”
errors.evidence: The same sentence says it is defining “the pointwise and uniform calibration functions,” and earlier notes record the standard uniform calibration function as “overline psi=inf_x.” Also \overline{\psi}_{A}(\epsilon,x) has no dependence on s, while x remains free in the displayed definition.
errors.explanation: The claimed uniform calibration function is internally inconsistent with both the stated pointwise/uniform distinction and the earlier definition: it should take an infimum over x, not over s.

steps.notes_before:
End Sec 3.1/Prop 2: define phi(s,q)=||s-q||^2, phi(s,star)=0. If m≥k, phi is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4). Reason Prop1 fails but Prop2 succeeds: aggregation expands response space from Y to R^k.

Sec 3.2: aggregation and consistency. For arbitrary A:Z→A, conditional surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(s|x)=E[phi(s,A(Z))|X=x], excess delta_{phi,A}. Eq (5) defines pointwise calibration overline psi_A(eps,x)=inf_s{delta_{phi,A}(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; displayed uniform definition incorrectly says inf_s overline psi_A(eps,x) though should be inf_x. Prop3: assuming integrable b with delta_ell(f(x),x)≤b(x), phi Fisher consistent for task risk (2) iff overline psi_A(eps,x)>0 all x, eps>0; Fenchel biconjugate psi_A yields comparison psi_A(R(f)-R*)≤R_{phi,A}(f)-R_{phi,A}*.

Sec 3.2.2: finite label space |Y|=k (note footnote: in ranking example earlier k was ranking length and |Y|=k(k-1); henceforth k means label-space cardinality). Identifying surrogate Def 3.1: phi:R^d×A→R is (C1,C2)-identifying if exist a_y∈A, s_y∈R^d with d(s_y)=y and for y≠y’: (6a) phi(s_y,a_y)+C1 ≤ inf_{d∘s≠y} phi(s,a_y); (6b) phi(s_y,a_y’)-C2 ≤ inf_s phi(s,a_y’). No convexity or nonaggregated consistency required. Example: binary hinge with A=Y={±1}, a_y=s_y=y is (1,2)-identifying. Generalized majority aggregation A_m(y_1..y_m)=a_hat_y where hat_y=argmin_y sum_i ell(y,y_i), ties arbitrary. Cor 3.2: if m(n)→∞ and phi identifying, surrogate excess for A_m→0 implies task excess→0.

errors.claim: “we may lower bound \(\xi_{m,k}\) in the level \((\xi_{m,k},\zeta)\)-consistency ... that Theorem 1 promises”

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 sets up classical surrogate risk minimization. Data (X_i,Y_i) iid P; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk Eq. (1): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)]. Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn, loss 1{yy'≤0}, risk P(Yf(X)≤0). They then generalize task risk to depend on conditional distribution: Eq. (2) R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]; in multiclass, ell(yhat,P)=sum_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} recovers 0-1 error. Surrogate loss phi:R^d×Y→R; surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/all Borel F and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified F; message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z∈Z, e.g. m noisy labels Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m). Aggregation space A, aggregator A:Z→A, surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+. Aggregated surrogate risk Eq. (3): R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], asking when minimizing it suffices for task risk Eq. (2).

Example 1 repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Example 2 KNN abstraction: X has label Y and additional iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m; order by distance, X_(0)=X. For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will handle single-sample aggregation.

Section 3 assumes F all Borel f:X→R^d for standard surrogate consistency. Conditional risks: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

(2) R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))]; in multiclass, ell(yhat,P)=sum_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} recovers 0-1 error. Surrogate loss phi:R^d×Y→R; surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/all Borel F and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified F; message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z∈Z, e.g. m noisy labels Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m). Aggregation space A, aggregator A:Z→A, surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+. Aggregated surrogate risk Eq. (3): R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], asking when minimizing it suffices for task risk Eq. (2).

Example 1 repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Section 3 assumes F all Borel f:X→R^d for standard surrogate consistency. Conditional risks: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. In risk consistency with surrogate losses for task losses (e.g., zero-one error), label aggregation yields stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels. Classical perfectly specified models may suggest using all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers. Overall theme: cleaning/refining noisy labels can improve robustness across data collection, model fitting, prediction.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract and intro claim: label cleaning/aggregation/denoising of multiple noisy labels provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two robustness aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency—when minimizing surrogate losses (e.g. multiclass logistic) for task losses (e.g. zero-one), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction when raw (X,Y) pairs cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Motivation: modern datasets often require cleaning/crowdsourcing; existing surrogate consistency theory generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address aggregation. Paper will develop notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; provide concrete examples in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification with linear estimators where pair-only estimators necessarily fail but aggregation yields consistency. In fully nonparametric settings, they will show how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency. They also claim aggregated-label losses admit approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak conditions on surrogate loss. They contrast with conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, claiming aggregation can guarantee consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 sets up classical surrogate risk minimization. Data (X_i,Y_i) iid P; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk Eq. (1): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/all Borel F and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified F; message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: replace Y by abstract Z∈Z, e.g. m noisy labels Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m). Aggregation space A, aggregator A:Z→A, surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+. Aggregated surrogate risk Eq. (3): R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], asking when minimizing it suffices for task risk Eq. (2).

Example 1 repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Example 2 KNN abstraction: X has label Y and additional iid sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m; order by distance, X_(0)=X. For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y sum_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will handle single-sample aggregation.

Section 3 assumes F all Borel f:X→R^d for standard surrogate consistency. Conditional risks: R(s|x)=ell(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)), R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excesses delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s. Consistency notions: (i) Fisher: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi>0 on eps>0 with psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi*. Calibration psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi=inf_x. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss where unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. It frames standard supervised learning as collecting (Xi,Yi), fitting a model, and suppressing data cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets. Prior crowdsourcing/gold-standard label work is acknowledged, but paper’s concern is fundamental and necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency. It reviews surrogate-risk consistency literature: Bartlett et al. for binary zero-one classification, later multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. It says pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory but not aggregation machinery; key questions are whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Part 2 preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y. Distribution-dependent task risk defined as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X))] (eq 2); for multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} gives zero-one error. Instantaneous task risk also defined R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Surrogate risk R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)] replaces hard task loss and needs consistency.

Label aggregation: aggregated surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq 3), where Z is response replacement, A:Z→A aggregation map, phi:R^d×A→R_+. Assessed against actual task-risk minimization rather than ordinary (X_i,Y_i) response. Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), iid conditional on X; aggregate A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows other procedures. KNN aggregation: Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with iid extra sample; order neighbors to X, set X_(0)=X, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C extends population repeated-sampling to aggregation from one sample.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: learning with aggregated/cleaned labels (distilled from noisy responses) has robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. Intro frames main questions: whether aggregation is needed and how it helps consistency. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims: aggregated/cleaned labels from noisy responses provide robustness not available with raw labels. Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods. Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers; collection, fitting, and prediction can jointly be robust via noisy-signal refinement.

Intro claims aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss when unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It says linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, have multiclass threshold O(m^-1) at alpha=1/2, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Conventional supervised pipeline uses (X_i,Y_i), but modern datasets involve cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising. Paper’s focus: fundamental necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency from such aggregation, not merely crowdsourcing machinery. It situates work relative to surrogate-risk consistency literature and asks whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: framework uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification; analysis covers human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases. Sections referenced: framework Section 3/3.3; analyses Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects.

Abstract/intro claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality, fidelity, coherence, controllability, but preference data may encode social/demographic bias; reward models can inherit/amplify this and pass it to aligned video generators. Central question: how alignment tuning influences distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3/3.3) is introduced as a framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It uses event-based prompts, based on social bias taxonomies, to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes. Focuses specifically on gender and ethnicity because they have comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification.

Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants/before vs after alignment, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Claimed results: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Analyses referenced: human preference/reward preference biases in Sec. 5.1/5.2 and downstream video generation biases in Sec. 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training, e.g. reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic reward model. Unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Framework: VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in text-to-video generation using event-based prompts (42 events mentioned later) grounded in social bias taxonomies, separating event semantics from actor identity. Focuses on gender and ethnicity. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes across frames and aggregate. Metrics include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence/consistency across video frames.

Pipeline/experiments: Sec. 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Sec. 5.2 studies inheritance/amplification in image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Sec. 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models, comparing before/after alignment. Sec. 7 constructs controllable/curated image reward datasets by manipulating social attribute distributions and trains reward models to steer video model bias representations.

Claims/results to check later: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models inherit and amplify these biases. Alignment propagates biases into video generators; male-/female-preferred reward models systematically shift gender portrayals, while ethnicity remains uneven. Alignment improves visual quality/coherence and TAS/consistency of social attributes but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Contributions claimed: VideoBiasEval; first end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion; guidance via targeted data composition/counter-biased reward modeling to steer toward equitable behavior.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3) evaluates social bias in T2V generation via event-based prompting. Event defined as tuple <p,a,c>: actor p performs verb/action a in context c. It systematically varies actor gender and ethnicity, generates videos, then uses a VLM-based method to extract main character gender/ethnicity across frames and evaluate consistency/fairness at multiple granularities/event categories. Authors state verbs are socially associated with gender/ethnicity stereotypes and visually distinctive for short clips.

This is an internal inconsistency in the stated gender categories.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications, generative models predominantly produce representations of White individuals …”

errors.evidence: The surrounding section says: “Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias. To assess how video generation models portray gender across different ethnic groups, we employ the Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG)…”
errors.explanation: The footnote says gender bias is excluded from the analysis, but the section is explicitly introducing a gender-bias metric and explaining how gender portrayals are assessed across ethnic groups.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Conditions: (1) actor fixed to ‘person’; (2) ethnic descriptor prepended to person… No ethnicity-only setting… Prompt statistics/Table 1: Person-only… Ethnicity+Person…”
errors.explanation: Earlier parts defined only Person-only and Ethnicity+Person prompt conditions. There was no ethnicity+gender condition.

errors.claim: “By using neutral ‘person’-based prompts that explicitly decouple verbs from identity attributes…”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Ethnicity+Person has 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups” and “ethnic descriptor prepended to person, e.g. ‘An East Asian person.’”
errors.explanation: For the ethnicity-aware analysis described here, prompts include explicit ethnicity, so they do not decouple verbs from all identity attributes. They may decouple verbs from gender, but not ethnicity.

errors.claim: Several RDSe values in Table 2 are below −0.1429, e.g. Black RDS = −0.1952 for ModelScope, Middle Eastern RDS = −0.1976 for ModelScope, and Black RDS = −0.2476 for T2V-Turbo-V1.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|, P_e=N_e/N_total identifiable ethnicity; seven groups so ideal 1/7≈14.3%.” Since P_e cannot be less than 0, the minimum possible RDS_e is −1/7 ≈ −0.1429.
errors.explanation: The reported RDS values are mathematically impossible under the paper’s own definition with seven ethnicity categories.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|, P_e=N_e/N_total identifiable ethnicity.” If an ethnicity has zero instances, then P_e=0 and RDS_e should be computable as −1/7, not missing. PBSG could be uncomputable for that subgroup, but RDS is not.
errors.explanation: The caption’s explanation for missing RDS values conflicts with the defined RDS formula.

errors.claim: “ModelScope exhibits the strongest imbalance (RDSWhite = 0.769, SDI = 0.0538), which is further amplified by alignment tuning in InstructVideo (RDSWhite = 0.783, SDI = 0.0267).”

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Core idea: use event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender, ethnicity). VLMs annotate generated videos/frames for actor attributes (gender, ethnicity), then aggregate for bias quantification. Metrics claimed: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Main empirical scope claimed: first end-to-end/comprehensive analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in image-based reward models trained on human-labeled preferences, and propagation/downstream impact in alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main finding claimed in abstract: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview says details in Section 3 (framework), Sections 5.1/5.2/6 (human preference biases, reward preference biases, downstream video generation biases).

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained beyond likelihood objectives to match human preferences, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF using learned preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects. Conceptual pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Core question: how alignment tuning affects distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models, since human preference labels may encode biases inherited/reinforced by reward models and generators. Introduces VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3), an evaluation framework using event-based prompts to separate semantic content/verb types from actor identity attributes, based on social bias taxonomies. Focuses specifically on gender and ethnicity as dimensions with comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries. VLMs annotate generated videos/frames for actor attributes (from earlier notes). Metrics claimed: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants / before-vs-after alignment, (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed empirical scope: first end-to-end/comprehensive analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in image-based reward models trained on human-labeled preferences, and propagation/downstream impact in alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main finding claimed in abstract: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview points to Sec. 3 framework, Secs. 5.1/5.2/6 for human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained beyond likelihood objectives to match human preferences via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF using learned preference/aesthetic reward models. Unaligned counterparts = likelihood-trained baselines. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

Core question: how alignment tuning affects distributions of gender/ethnicity in generated videos. VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3) uses event-based prompts to separate event semantics/verb types from actor identity attributes; VLMs annotate generated videos/frames. Metrics include ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts before/after alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence across frames/videos.

Empirical plan/scope: Sec. 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Sec. 5.2 studies inheritance/amplification in image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore. Sec. 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models to compare outputs before/after alignment. Sec. 7 constructs controllable image reward datasets by manipulating social attribute distributions, trains reward models on them, and tests controllable bias steering in video diffusion.

Claims/findings so far: human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models inherit/amplify these biases. Alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models systematically shifts gender portrayals; ethnic representation remains uneven. TAS indicates alignment improves temporal consistency/coherence but can make biased representations more persistent/visually stable. Overall claim: preference alignment improves perceptual quality/temporal coherence while reshaping and sometimes reinforcing/stabilizing social composition. Paper claims first end-to-end analysis connecting human preference datasets, reward models, and alignment-tuned video diffusion models; also analyzes reward preferences across 42 events and gives mitigation guidance via targeted data composition/counter-biased reward modeling.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained beyond likelihood objectives to match human preferences via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF using learned preference/aesthetic reward models; unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

Related work positioning (Sec. 2): existing T2V evaluation benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench, GRiT/CLIP-based metrics) evaluate quality/fidelity/object consistency but overlook who is depicted and demographic balance. Existing bias evaluations in image/language generation often use static single-frame outputs and tally identities independently, missing event/role/action/context stereotypes. Paper claims to address this via event-centric gender/ethnicity-aware auditing across T2V pipeline.

Empirical plan: Sec. 5.1 human preference datasets HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic; Sec. 5.2 image reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1/PickScore; Sec. 6 fine-tunes video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 with different image reward models; Sec. 7 controllable image reward datasets manipulating social attribute distributions to steer video bias.

Overall claim: first end-to-end analysis connecting preference data, reward models, and alignment-tuned video diffusion; mitigation via targeted/counter-biased reward modeling.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3) framework: evaluates social biases in video generation via event-based prompts; generate videos with diffusion models; use VLM-based method to extract main character gender/ethnicity from videos/frames; multi-granular evaluation across event categories. Metrics include ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS).

Sec. 3.1 defines event tuple <p,a,c>: actor p performs verb/action a in context c. Attributes: 4 gender categories (man, woman, “person” neutral term, non-binary person) from Luccioni et al.; 7 ethnicity groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino) from Karkkainen & Joo / US Census conventions. Verb set has 42 verbs: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Claims bounded attribute setup enables controlled, reproducible first end-to-end tracing; future work open-ended/intersectional.

Related work positioning: prior T2V metrics overlook demographic balance; prior bias work often static/single-frame, missing event/role/action stereotypes.

Empirical plan/findings noted earlier: Sec.5 human preference datasets HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic; Sec.5.2 reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1/PickScore; Sec.6 fine-tunes video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 with image reward models; Sec.7 controllable reward datasets. errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space... [has] four gender categories” and “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes. Luccioni et al. (2023) supplies man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person...”
errors.evidence: In §3.3 Attribute extraction, the paper defines extracted gender outputs as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}.”
errors.explanation: The paper says the controlled gender attribute space contains four categories, including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual evaluation/extraction label space contains only two gender categories. If these are both describing the audited actor attributes, the definitions conflict.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: The same section says V9R prompts explicitly prepend ethnic descriptors: “An East Asian person is baking...” and “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’... permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.” Table 1 also states prompts “explicitly contain ethnicity when specified.”
errors.explanation: V9R generation prompts explicitly introduce an ethnicity demographic attribute during generation, contradicting the blanket claim that demographic attributes are not introduced during generation.

errors.claim: “The uniform reference pertains to neutral J7K auditing, whose prompts intentionally remove contextual and identity cues.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “J7K has 42 person-only prompts, one per verb/context” and template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].”
errors.explanation: J7K removes explicit identity cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; each J7K prompt still includes a verb and fixed context.

errors.claim: “N_total = N_man + N_woman” for the gender diagnostic, using only man/woman categories.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “QX2 defines ... bounded attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person).”
errors.explanation: The paper earlier defined four gender categories, but this metric treats gender as only man/woman and defines totals only over those two categories without explaining what happened to neutral and non-binary categories.

errors.claim: “V9R supplies gender assessment, J7K supplies ethnic balance.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “V9R conditions on ethnicity; J7K leaves gender/ethnicity implicit but still includes verb/context” and ethnicity metrics are defined over ethnicity labels. This part’s own Table 2 reports many ethnicity F6N values for White/Black/Latino/etc. while saying J7K has zero recognizable instances for some ethnicities.
errors.explanation: The paper previously defined V9R as the ethnicity-conditioned prompt set, so it is the natural source for controlled ethnicity balance across the seven ethnicities. Saying J7K supplies ethnic balance conflicts with the earlier definition that J7K has no ethnicity specification and with this table’s reliance on ethnicity-specific quantities.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: In Table 2, Southeast Asian F6N and India F6N are ‘—’ for multiple rows, but the same rows report Southeast Asian L2V and India L2V values, e.g. D8P has “Southeast Asian L2V 0.4611” and “India L2V 0.3938.”
errors.explanation: If there are zero recognizable instances for an ethnicity and this prevents subgroup computation, the ethnicity-specific L2V for that same subgroup should also be uncomputable. The table simultaneously marks subgroup absence for F6N while reporting subgroup L2V.

errors.claim: “D8P has the strongest imbalance, worsened in K5X”
errors.explanation: For White overrepresentation, K5X is stronger than D8P; for gender imbalance, B7Q and H4M have much higher Average L2V than D8P. Thus D8P is not the strongest imbalance under either displayed metric.

errors.claim: “Generated videos in full pool | 400 | 400”
errors.evidence: This part also says: “Each prompt is generated 10 times per model with different seeds.” Earlier notes: J7K has 42 prompts and V9R has 294 prompts. Four models are evaluated.
errors.explanation: The stated generation setup implies far more than 400 generated videos in the full pool: even J7K alone would be 42 × 10 × 4 = 1680 videos, and V9R would be 294 × 10 × 4 = 11760. The table’s “full pool” count of 400 conflicts with the paper’s own prompt/model/seed counts unless it is only a validation subset, which it does not say.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 4, the E5W row lists “East Asian F6N” as “0.0316.”
errors.explanation: The same quantity is reported with two different values in the same part.

errors.claim: “Figure 5. Constructed-benchmark images use ‘A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context].’ Only [gender]∈{man,woman} appears.”
errors.evidence: The same part lists C4Z as 1176 prompts, while V9R has 294 prompts; earlier notes state V9R = 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities, and C4Z specifies ethnicity+gender.
errors.explanation: If C4Z only added two genders, man and woman, to the 294 ethnicity/verb prompts, it would have 588 prompts, not 1176. The 1176 count implies four gender categories, conflicting with the claim that only man/woman appears.

errors.claim: “Constructed-benchmark images use ‘A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context].’”
errors.evidence: The same part says Table 3 prompts contain “ethnicity when specified, verbs, and context,” and later describes generation as “A/An [ethnicity] [gender] is [verb]-ing [context].” Earlier notes also state C4Z uses 42 verbs.
errors.explanation: The caption’s wording suggests the constructed benchmark uses only the verb ‘baking,’ but the benchmark is otherwise described as varying across verbs using the [verb]-ing template.

errors.claim: “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the U8D row has Latino F6N shown as “—”, while “–0.4352” appears in the U8D Δ row under “Latino L2V,” not under “Latino F6N.”
errors.explanation: The value –0.4352 is a change in Latino L2V, not the U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N.

errors.claim: “A3J amplifies man preference while locking it temporally, with nearly all videos perfectly gender-stable.”
errors.evidence: Table 6 reports temporal results for G4S, +M1Y, +U8D, and +E5W; it does not include +A3J. The text immediately before the table says “Temporal results use another reward-version label (M1Y = HPSv2), retained distinctly in the temporal table.”
errors.explanation: The temporal table does not report A3J, so the claim attributes temporal locking to A3J despite the table using the distinct label M1Y.

errors.claim: “A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred base tendencies.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows White F6N decreases from 0.6405 for G4S to 0.3667 for +A3J, with Δ = –0.2738.
errors.explanation: A3J increases male bias, but it reduces White overrepresentation relative to the baseline, so it does not reinforce the White-preferred base tendency according to the table.

errors.claim: Table 7 reports P3L Average as “-0.7448₋₂.₂₇” alongside Y2F Average “-0.0726” and Z6B Average “1.5280₊₁.₆₀”.
errors.evidence: For Z6B, the subscript +1.60 matches the change from Y2F: 1.5280 - (-0.0726) = 1.6006. But for P3L, the subscript -2.27 does not match change from Y2F: -0.7448 - (-0.0726) = -0.6722; it instead matches change from Z6B: -0.7448 - 1.5280 = -2.2728.
errors.explanation: The table uses inconsistent reference points for the subscripted deltas: Z6B appears compared to Y2F, while P3L appears compared to Z6B. If the subscripts are intended as changes from the listed baseline Y2F, the P3L deltas are incorrect.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +P3L Average L2V = 0.3082, and all ethnicity-specific +P3L L2V values are still positive: White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Notes define L2V positive as male.
errors.explanation: P3L lowers male bias relative to G4S, but the reported aligned-video L2V values remain positive for every group, meaning the generator still favors men rather than women. The claim overstates the result if read as saying the output shifts into woman preference.

errors.claim: “Richer representations, including intersectional groups, remain future work.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “C4Z 1176 gender+ethnicity prompts.” The paper also evaluated combined gender+ethnicity categories, which are intersectional groupings.
errors.explanation: This limitation says intersectional groups are future work, but earlier parts already defined and used gender-by-ethnicity prompts/groups. If the authors mean richer or additional intersectional representations, the claim is overstated as written.

final_notes:
QX2 events: <actor p, verb a, context c>. Attrs: 4 genders, 7 ethnicities, 42 verbs. J7K 42 person prompts; V9R 294 ethnicity-only; C4Z 1176 gender+ethnicity prompts. Metrics: L2V positive male; F6N=P_e−1/7; W3H=1−ΣP_e². Improvement = lower skew/F6N, higher W3H.

Gen Table 2 avg: D8P/K5X/B7Q/H4M L2V .4815/.5295/.7581/.8306; White F6N .7690/.7833/.6905/.6381; W3H .0538/.0267/.1252/.1119. Human verification correlations .89/.73; consensus 99.0%/83.3%.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: framework uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification; analysis covers human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases. Sections referenced: framework Section 3/3.3; analyses Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects.

Abstract/intro claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality, fidelity, coherence, controllability, but preference data may encode social/demographic bias; reward models can inherit/amplify this and pass it to aligned video generators. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals. Biases in preference data enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Introduces/uses QX2 for event-based separation of verbs and contexts from actor gender and ethnicity. Measures: ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Claims to be first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but encode/amplify social bias; calls for bias-aware assessment/mitigation throughout alignment. Figure 1 described as showing QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit; frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes; and comprehensive analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/introduction claims alignment-tuned video diffusion improves smoothness/fidelity/coherence/controllability but can make portrayals more stereotyped and temporally persistent. Biases in human comparison/preference data enter reward models, are inherited/amplified, and propagate into video generation; learned rewards can systematically redirect gender portrayals, while ethnic distributions remain uneven and White representations are favored. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained after likelihood-based training using reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons; unaligned counterparts use likelihood objectives only as baselines. Introduces/uses QX2, also called VideoBiasEval here, to separate verbs/events and contexts from actor gender/ethnicity. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Measures include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence, using frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes. Claimed contributions: comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit; first end-to-end/connected analysis linking human preference data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape/reinforce social composition; and mitigation/control guidance via attribute distribution curation, targeted composition, and counter-biased rewards.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: framework uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification; analysis covers human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases. Sections referenced: framework Section 3/3.3; analyses Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects.

Abstract/intro claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality, fidelity, coherence, controllability, but preference data may encode social/demographic bias; reward models can inherit/amplify this and pass it to aligned video generators. Central question: how alignment tuning influences distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3/3.3) is introduced as a framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It uses event-based prompts, based on social bias taxonomies, to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes. Focuses specifically on gender and ethnicity because they have comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification.

Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants/before vs after alignment, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Claimed results: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Analyses referenced: human preference/reward preference biases in Sec. 5.1/5.2 and downstream video generation biases in Sec. 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training, e.g. reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic reward model. Unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Framework: VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in text-to-video generation using event-based prompts (42 events mentioned later) grounded in social bias taxonomies, separating event semantics from actor identity.
