errors.explanation: The paper says the controlled gender attribute space contains four categories, including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual evaluation/extraction label space contains only two gender categories. If these are both describing the audited actor attributes, the definitions conflict.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: The same section says V9R prompts explicitly prepend ethnic descriptors: “An East Asian person is baking...” and “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’... permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.” Table 1 also states prompts “explicitly contain ethnicity when specified.”
errors.explanation: V9R generation prompts explicitly introduce an ethnicity demographic attribute during generation, contradicting the blanket claim that demographic attributes are not introduced during generation.

errors.claim: “The uniform reference pertains to neutral J7K auditing, whose prompts intentionally remove contextual and identity cues.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “J7K has 42 person-only prompts, one per verb/context” and template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].”
errors.explanation: J7K removes explicit identity cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; each J7K prompt still includes a verb and fixed context.

errors.claim: “N_total = N_man + N_woman” for the gender diagnostic, using only man/woman categories.

errors.explanation: The paper earlier defined four gender categories, but this metric treats gender as only man/woman and defines totals only over those two categories without explaining what happened to neutral and non-binary categories.

errors.explanation: The paper previously defined V9R as the ethnicity-conditioned prompt set, so it is the natural source for controlled ethnicity balance across the seven ethnicities. Saying J7K supplies ethnic balance conflicts with the earlier definition that J7K has no ethnicity specification and with this table’s reliance on ethnicity-specific quantities.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”

errors.explanation: If there are zero recognizable instances for an ethnicity and this prevents subgroup computation, the ethnicity-specific L2V for that same subgroup should also be uncomputable. The table simultaneously marks subgroup absence for F6N while reporting subgroup L2V.

errors.claim: “D8P has the strongest imbalance, worsened in K5X”

errors.claim: Several F6N entries in Table 5 are below –1/7, e.g. “Middle Eastern F6N -0.3667” for +A3J and “Middle Eastern F6N -0.4286” for +U8D.

errors.claim: “A3J amplifies man preference while locking it temporally, with nearly all videos perfectly gender-stable.”

errors.explanation: The part makes a specific temporal claim about A3J, but the temporal table in this part does not report A3J. The claim is not supported by the table it summarizes and appears to refer to an unreported condition.

errors.claim: Table 7 reports reward-model L2V values such as “Z6B | Average | 1.5280” and White “1.6300.”

errors.explanation: If these are L2V preference-bias scores under the paper’s own definition, values above 1 are impossible.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”

final_notes:
QX2 events: <actor p, verb a, context c>. Bounded attrs: 4 genders, 7 ethnicities, 42 verbs/actions. J7K: 42 person-only prompts; V9R: 294=42×7 ethnicities. C4Z inconsistency: Table says 1176 but ethnicity+gender{man,woman}+verb/context implies 588; also C4Z intersectional prompt set conflicts with final limitation that intersectional groups remain future work.

Extraction: 3 VLM judges classify 16 frames/video. Gender binary man/woman; ethnicity 7 groups. TAS=% frames matching final video label.

Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, range [-1,1]. Ethnicity F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7, range [-1/7,6/7]. W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e². Δ improvement = more balanced gender, less ethnic skew, higher diversity.

Table 2: D8P/K5X/B7Q/H4M avg L2V .4815/.5295/.7581/.8306; White F6N .7690/.7833/.6905/.6381; W3H .0538/.0267/.1252/.1119. Human verification correlations .89/.73.

Reward data: HPDv2 men preferred 79.23%, White 43.34%; Pick-a-Pic women 61.11%, White 40.08%. Table 4: Y2F avg L2V -0.0726 W3H .8495; A3J .6039 .8492; U8D -0.0984 .8470; E5W -0.1157 .8483; East Asian F6N conflict .0316/.0352.

Table 5: G4S avg L2V .8034 W3H .1433; +A3J .9116/.1257; +U8D .2267/.0976; +E5W .3714/.1467. Impossible F6N below -1/7; U8D Latino -0.4352 mislabeled F6N though ΔL2V. Table 6 temporal: no A3J row.

Table7 reward L2V: Y2F -0.0726; Z6B 1.5280 impossible; P3L -0.7448. Table8 G4S .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082 still male despite text saying shifts toward woman.

Part12 broader impact: alignment/RLHF can stabilize bias; supplementary inventory lists per-verb gender/ethnicity, training-data effects, statistical analyses, reward/video implementation and training details. Acknowledgment: funding/support only, no technical claims.

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals. Biases in preference data enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Introduces/uses QX2 for event-based separation of verbs and contexts from actor gender and ethnicity. Measures: ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Claims to be first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but encode/amplify social bias; calls for bias-aware assessment/mitigation throughout alignment. Figure 1 described as showing QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit; frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes; and comprehensive analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/introduction claims alignment-tuned video diffusion improves smoothness/fidelity/coherence/controllability but can make portrayals more stereotyped and temporally persistent. Biases in human comparison/preference data enter reward models, are inherited/amplified, and propagate into video generation; learned rewards can systematically redirect gender portrayals, while ethnic distributions remain uneven and White representations are favored. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained after likelihood-based training using reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons; unaligned counterparts use likelihood objectives only as baselines. Introduces/uses QX2, also called VideoBiasEval here, to separate verbs/events and contexts from actor gender/ethnicity. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Measures include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence, using frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes. Claimed contributions: comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit; first end-to-end/connected analysis linking human preference data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape/reinforce social composition; and mitigation/control guidance via attribute distribution curation, targeted composition, and counter-biased rewards.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: framework uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification; analysis covers human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases. Sections referenced: framework Section 3/3.3; analyses Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects.

Abstract/intro claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality, fidelity, coherence, controllability, but preference data may encode social/demographic bias; reward models can inherit/amplify this and pass it to aligned video generators. Central question: how alignment tuning influences distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3/3.3) is introduced as a framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It uses event-based prompts, based on social bias taxonomies, to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes. Focuses specifically on gender and ethnicity because they have comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification.

Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants/before vs after alignment, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Claimed results: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Analyses referenced: human preference/reward preference biases in Sec. 5.1/5.2 and downstream video generation biases in Sec. 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training, e.g. reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic reward model. Unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Framework: VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in text-to-video generation using event-based prompts (42 events mentioned later) grounded in social bias taxonomies, separating event semantics from actor identity. Focuses on gender and ethnicity. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes across frames and aggregate. Metrics include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence/consistency across video frames.

Pipeline/experiments: Sec. 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Sec. 5.2 studies inheritance/amplification in image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Sec. 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models, comparing before/after alignment. Sec. 7 constructs controllable/curated image reward datasets by manipulating social attribute distributions and trains reward models to steer video model bias representations.

Claims/results to check later: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models inherit and amplify these biases. Alignment propagates biases into video generators; male-/female-preferred reward models systematically shift gender portrayals, while ethnicity remains uneven. Alignment improves visual quality/coherence and TAS/consistency of social attributes but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Contributions claimed: VideoBiasEval; first end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion; guidance via targeted data composition/counter-biased reward modeling to steer toward equitable behavior.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3) evaluates social bias in T2V generation via event-based prompting. Event defined as tuple <p,a,c>: actor p performs verb/action a in context c. It systematically varies actor gender and ethnicity, generates videos, then uses a VLM-based method to extract main character gender/ethnicity across frames and evaluate consistency/fairness at multiple granularities/event categories. Metrics from earlier notes include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS).

Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, neutral “person,” non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verbs listed: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Authors state verbs are socially associated with gender/ethnicity stereotypes and visually distinctive for short clips.

Experimental roadmap from earlier: Sec. 5.1 analyzes HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic demographic preferences; Sec. 5.2 reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1/PickScore inherit/amplify biases; Sec. 6 fine-tunes VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model with image reward models; Sec. 7 uses curated reward datasets to steer bias. Key claimed findings to check: preference datasets and reward models favor White/non-neutral gender patterns; alignment propagates biases, shifts gender according to reward model, ethnicity remains uneven; alignment improves quality/coherence/TAS but may stabilize biased depictions.

QX2 events <actor p, verb a, context c>; attributes 4 genders, 7 ethnicities, 42 verbs. Prompts: J7K 42 person-only; V9R 294 ethnicity-only; C4Z 1176 ethnicity+gender. Extraction: 3 VLM judges, 16 frames/video; TAS. Metrics: gender L2V=(Nman−Nwoman)/sum; ethnicity F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7; W3H=1−ΣP_e². Table2 video pairs: Avg L2V .4815/.5295/.7581/.8306; White F6N .7690/.7833/.6905/.6381; W3H .0538/.0267/.1252/.1119. Human verification corr .89 gender/.73 ethnicity.
Reward datasets: R9C/HPDv2 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs, 26 valid gender-pair verbs, Men 69.23% (18/26), White 43.34%. N6T/Pick-a-Pic 14,958 tuples, 19 verbs, 18 valid; table says Women 51.11% (11/18), arithmetic conflict since 11/18=61.11; White 40.08%. Reward Table4: Y2F avg L2V -0.0726 W3H .8495; A3J .6039/.8492; U8D -.0984/.8470; E5W -.1157/.8483. E5W East Asian F6N conflict .0316 vs .0352. Reward scoring: standardized scalar gender L2V=male score−female; ethnicity softmax.
Table5 G4S baseline Avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433; +A3J .9116/.1257; +U8D .2267/.0976; +E5W .3714/.1467. Error: “U8D Latino F6N –0.4352” actually Latino L2V delta. Table6 G4S ethnicity/gender T8Q .8904/.9763; M1Y/U8D/E5W improve stability.
Controllable gender preference: Z6B/RMM man-preferred and P3L/RMW woman-preferred, each 2.94M C4Z image pairs + 537,660 R9C. Table7 L2V: Y2F -0.0726; Z6B 1.5280; P3L -0.7448. Table8 G4S aligned L2V: baseline .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082. Error: text says +P3L shifts toward woman preference, but L2Vs remain positive.
Conclusion/limitations/broader impact: fixed taxonomy, VLM judge bias, limited experiments; alignment/RLHF may stabilize/entrench bias; preference data dual-use; need QX2-like audits. Acknowledgment lists funding/support and standard disclaimer.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals. Biases in preference data enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Introduces/uses QX2 for event-based separation of verbs and contexts from actor gender and ethnicity. Measures: ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Claims to be first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but encode/amplify social bias; calls for bias-aware assessment/mitigation throughout alignment. Figure 1 described as showing QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit; frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes; and comprehensive analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/introduction claims alignment-tuned video diffusion improves smoothness/fidelity/coherence/controllability but can make portrayals more stereotyped and temporally persistent. Biases in human comparison/preference data enter reward models, are inherited/amplified, and propagate into video generation; learned rewards can systematically redirect gender portrayals, while ethnic distributions remain uneven and White representations are favored. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained after likelihood-based training using reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons; unaligned counterparts use likelihood objectives only as baselines. Introduces/uses QX2, also called VideoBiasEval here, to separate verbs/events and contexts from actor gender/ethnicity. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Measures include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence, using frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes. Claimed contributions: comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit; first end-to-end/connected analysis linking human preference data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape/reinforce social composition; and mitigation/control guidance via attribute distribution curation, targeted composition, and counter-biased rewards.

Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. QX2 events: <actor p, verb a, context c>. Claimed attrs: 4 gender categories, 7 ethnic groups, 42 verbs/actions. J7K: 42 person-only prompts; V9R: 294=42×7; C4Z Table 3 says 1176 prompts but Fig 5 implies gender {man,woman}=588 and fixes “is baking [context]” conflicting with 42 verbs.

Extraction: 3 VLM judges on 16 uniform frames/video; binary gender {man,woman}, ethnicity 7 groups. Metrics: L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male. Ethnicity F6N=P_e−1/7; W3H=1−ΣP_e².

Part 6 Table 2: D8P/K5X/B7Q/H4M avg L2V .4815,.5295,.7581,.8306; White F6N .7690,.7833,.6905,.6381; W3H .0538,.0267,.1252,.1119.

Part 9 Table 5 G4S aligned: baseline avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433; +A3J .9116/.3667/.1257; +U8D .2267/.4286/.0976; +E5W .3714/.6833/.1467. U8D Latino F6N misreported as -0.4352; A3J does not reinforce White preference.

Conclusion/limitations/broader impact: calls for bias auditing/mitigation; limitations include fixed socially constructed gender/ethnicity categories, VLM judge bias, limited alignment/rewards, limited synthetic gender-preference manipulation, fixed action taxonomy. Biases in preference data enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Introduces/uses QX2 for event-based separation of verbs and contexts from actor gender and ethnicity. Measures: ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Claims to be first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Figure 1 described as showing QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit; frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes; and comprehensive analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/introduction claims alignment-tuned video diffusion improves smoothness/fidelity/coherence/controllability but can make portrayals more stereotyped and temporally persistent. Biases in human comparison/preference data enter reward models, are inherited/amplified, and propagate into video generation; learned rewards can systematically redirect gender portrayals, while ethnic distributions remain uneven and White representations are favored. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained after likelihood-based training using reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons; unaligned counterparts use likelihood objectives only as baselines. Introduces/uses QX2, also called VideoBiasEval here, to separate verbs/events and contexts from actor gender/ethnicity. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Measures include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence, using frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes. Claimed contributions: comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit; first end-to-end/connected analysis linking human preference data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape/reinforce social composition; and mitigation/control guidance via attribute distribution curation, targeted composition, and counter-biased rewards.

final_notes:
Title: “From Preferences to Prejudice...” Aligned = preference/RLHF/reward-tuned video diffusion models; unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines. Sec.3/4 prompt inconsistency: said 4 genders, 7 ethnicities, 42 verbs; later Person-only=42, Ethnicity+Person=294, Ethnicity+Gender=1176, no clear gender condition; video gender labels only {man,woman}. PBSG=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, bounded [-1,1]; positive=man bias, negative=woman bias. Table2 avg PBSG: ModelScope .4815, InstructVideo .5295; VideoCrafter .7581, T2V .8306. Human sensitivity claim SDI .745→.761 conflicts with Table2 scale/values.

Sec.5.1 datasets: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs; elsewhere says 42 verbs. Gender filtering: HPDv2 26/42 verbs, 69.23% men-preferred; Pick-a-Pic 18/42, 61.11% women-preferred. Ethnicity preference: White 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic. Table4 image reward: CLIP PBSG -0.0726; HPS2.0 0.6039; HPS2.1 -0.0984; PickScore -0.1157. HPS2.1 training data undisclosed yet text says shifts align with each model’s training data.

Sec.6 VCM-VC2: base PBSG .8034 SDI .1433; HPS2.0 .9116/.1257; HPS2.1 .2267/.0976; PickScore .3714/.1467. Text mislabeled Latino RDS=-.4352; table has it as Δ Latino PBSG. Table6: alignment improves TAS/perfect stability.

Sec.7: constructs man/woman-preferred reward datasets: 29.4M Ethnicity+Gender pairs + 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table7 reward “PBSG” has RMM >1, impossible if PBSG definition applies. Table8: RMM raises VCM PBSG to .9584; RMW lowers to .3082 but all values remain positive, so not woman-preference despite text saying strong shift toward woman-preference bias.

Final acknowledgment: funders listed; no substantive results.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: framework uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification; analysis covers human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases. Sections referenced: framework Section 3/3.3; analyses Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects.

Abstract/intro claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality, fidelity, coherence, controllability, but preference data may encode social/demographic bias; reward models can inherit/amplify this and pass it to aligned video generators. Central question: how alignment tuning influences distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3/3.3) is introduced as a framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It uses event-based prompts, based on social bias taxonomies, to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes. Focuses specifically on gender and ethnicity because they have comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification.

Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants/before vs after alignment, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Claimed results: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Analyses referenced: human preference/reward preference biases in Sec. 5.1/5.2 and downstream video generation biases in Sec. 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training, e.g. reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic reward model. Unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Framework: VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in text-to-video generation using event-based prompts (42 events mentioned later) grounded in social bias taxonomies, separating event semantics from actor identity. Focuses on gender and ethnicity. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes across frames and aggregate. Metrics include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence/consistency across video frames.

Pipeline/experiments: Sec. 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Sec. 5.2 studies inheritance/amplification in image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Sec. 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models, comparing before/after alignment. Sec. 7 constructs controllable/curated image reward datasets by manipulating social attribute distributions and trains reward models to steer video model bias representations.

Claims/results to check later: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models inherit and amplify these biases. Alignment propagates biases into video generators; male-/female-preferred reward models systematically shift gender portrayals, while ethnicity remains uneven. Alignment improves visual quality/coherence and TAS/consistency of social attributes but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Contributions claimed: VideoBiasEval; first end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion; guidance via targeted data composition/counter-biased reward modeling to steer toward equitable behavior.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training, e.g. reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic reward model. Unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Metrics include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence/consistency across frames. Related work section claims existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench; GRiT/CLIP metrics) overlook depicted identities/demographic balance; existing generative bias benchmarks mostly tally static identity frequencies and miss event/role/temporal stereotypes. Their claimed novelty: event-centric gender/ethnicity-aware auditing across T2V pipeline.

Pipeline/experiments: Sec. 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Sec. 5.2 studies inheritance/amplification in image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Metrics from earlier notes include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS).

Reward datasets: R9C/HPDv2 men preferred 69.23%, White 43.34%; N6T/Pick-a-Pic women preferred 61.11%, White 40.08%. Reward models: Y2F=CLIP, A3J=HPSv2.0/R9C, U8D=HPSv2.1/X7H, E5W=PickScore/N6T. V9R conditions on ethnicity; J7K leaves gender/ethnicity implicit but still includes verb/context. §3.3 parity/uniform baselines are diagnostic, not real-world truth.

Attribute extraction: 3 VLM judges classify 16 uniformly sampled frames/video. Defined extraction outputs binary gender G={man,woman} and ethnicity E=7; frame majority within model gives video labels, then fused. TAS = % frames matching final majority-voted video label; high = coherent identity, low = flicker.

Current metrics: L2V/PBSG = (N_man − N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, negative female, 0 balanced; computed per verb and ethnicity; gender-only analysis excluded because unspecified ethnicity allegedly mostly White. Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total over identifiable ethnicity; F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/7; W3H/SDI = 1 − ΣP_e². Shifts: ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, ΔW3H; improvement = more balanced gender, less ethnic skew, higher diversity.

Internal issues noted: four gender categories claimed but extraction/metrics only man/woman; “demographic attributes not introduced during generation” conflicts with V9R ethnicity-conditioned prompts; current part falsely says J7K removes contextual cues though J7K includes verb/context.

errors.claim: “V9R supplies gender assessment, J7K supplies ethnic balance.”

errors.explanation: The paper previously defined V9R as the ethnicity-conditioned prompt set, so it is the natural source for controlled ethnicity balance across the seven ethnicities. errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”

errors.explanation: If there are zero recognizable instances for an ethnicity and this prevents subgroup computation, the ethnicity-specific L2V for that same subgroup should also be uncomputable. The table simultaneously marks subgroup absence for F6N while reporting subgroup L2V.

errors.claim: “D8P has the strongest imbalance, worsened in K5X”

sol_grade.reason: None of the reported errors challenges the 29.4 million pair count or identifies that seven ethnicities, 42 verbs, and 100 images per gender yield only 2.94 million pairs.

errors.claim: “we define two prompting conditions: (1) Person-only ... 42 total; and (2) Ethnicity+Person ... 294 prompts” and VLMs output gender labels only “G={man, woman}.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “VideoBiasEval ... systematically varies actor gender and ethnicity” and “Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, neutral ‘person,’ non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups ...”
errors.explanation: This part describes only person-only and ethnicity+person prompt conditions, with no man/woman/non-binary actor prompts, and reduces gender classification to binary man/woman. That conflicts with the earlier stated controlled attribute space of four gender categories and systematic variation of actor gender.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications, generative models predominantly produce representations of White individuals...”
errors.location: this part, footnote under Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias
errors.evidence: The section is explicitly titled “Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias” and says “we employ the Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG)” and then defines PBSG as measuring male vs. female representations.
errors.explanation: The footnote says gender bias is excluded, but the surrounding text says this analysis is specifically a gender-bias analysis. This is an internal contradiction within the part.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: the prompt set has only Person-only = 42 prompts and Ethnicity+Person = 294 prompts; “No explicit gender-prompt condition is described here.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously described an ethnicity+person condition, not an ethnicity+gender condition. This claim introduces a condition that conflicts with the earlier prompt design notes.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: “RDSe = Pe - 1/|E|, Pe = Ne/N_total identifiable ethnicity; with 7 groups uniform=14.3%.” If a group has zero recognizable instances, Pe = 0, so RDSe would be computable as -1/7 ≈ -0.143, not uncomputable.
errors.explanation: The paper’s own metric definition implies zero representation yields a valid RDSe value, so saying zero recognizable instances prevent metric computation conflicts with the stated formula.

errors.claim: “InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1 exhibit PBSG increases of 0.04 and 0.0725, respectively.”
errors.location: this part, Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias paragraph
errors.evidence: Table 2 Δ row for ModelScope → InstructVideo gives Average PBSG change as +0.0480, not +0.04; T2V-Turbo-V1 is +0.0725.
errors.explanation: The stated InstructVideo increase does not match the table’s reported average ΔPBSG.

errors.claim: “ModelScope exhibits the strongest imbalance (RDSWhite = 0.769, SDI = 0.0538), which is further amplified by alignment tuning in InstructVideo (RDSWhite = 0.783, SDI = 0.0267).”
errors.evidence: The same sentence reports InstructVideo has higher White overrepresentation and lower diversity than ModelScope: RDSWhite 0.783 > 0.769 and SDI 0.0267 < 0.0538.
errors.explanation: If InstructVideo is more imbalanced by both cited metrics, ModelScope cannot be the strongest imbalance among the models as worded.

errors.claim: “all core bias metrics remain statistically stable when restricting to this subset (e.g., PBS_G: 0.846 → 0.863 ...; SDI: 0.745 → 0.761)”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 2 notes report video-output SDI values of 0.0538, 0.0267, 0.1252, and 0.1119 for the evaluated models, and PBSG averages of 0.4815, 0.5295, 0.7581, and 0.8306.
errors.explanation: The quoted “core bias metrics” are presented as the reported bias measurements, but the SDI value 0.745 is far outside and inconsistent with the earlier reported SDI values for the video-output bias evaluation, and PBS_G 0.846 does not correspond to the earlier listed averages except only roughly to one model. The part does not specify a different metric setting that would reconcile these numbers.

errors.claim: “Figure 3: Image reward datasets gender preference distribution across 42 verbs” / “Figure 4: Image reward datasets ethnicity preference across 42 verbs” and “Figure 3 shows the gender preference bias across 42 verbs in the two datasets.”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same section: “After processing, HPDv2 contains 28,783 ... tuples covering 29 verbs, and Pick-a-Pic contains 14,958 across 19 verbs.”
errors.explanation: The text says the processed datasets cover only 29 and 19 verbs, but then describes the dataset preference distributions as being across 42 verbs. Unless zero/absent verbs are explicitly included, this is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “Using the event prompting templates introduced in Section 3.2 ... The benchmark includes ... (2) Ethnicity+Gender, where both gender and ethnicity are explicitly indicated.”
errors.evidence: Notes from earlier parts: “Later prompt description only Person-only=42 prompts and Ethnicity+Person=294 prompts; no explicit gender-prompt condition, though another part said ‘ethnicity+gender condition.’”
errors.explanation: This part says the Ethnicity+Gender setting uses templates introduced in Section 3.2, but the recorded Section 3.2 prompt settings did not include an explicit gender-prompt condition.

errors.claim: “The base model, CLIP, slightly favors White individuals (RDS = 0.0182) and achieves the lowest SDI score (0.8495)”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 4 notes: “Overall SDI ~0.8495, .8492, .8470, .8483” for CLIP, HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore respectively.
errors.explanation: CLIP’s SDI of 0.8495 is higher than the other reported SDI values, not the lowest. This also conflicts with the immediately stated rule that higher SDI means more balanced/diverse outputs.

errors.claim: “Under the ethnicity-only condition, we analyze models’ representation balance using the previously defined RDSe and SDI metrics.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 caption says missing values indicate cases under “the person-only condition (i.e., when ethnicity is not explicitly specified).”
errors.explanation: The paragraph says the ethnicity representation metrics are analyzed under an “ethnicity-only” condition, but the table caption describes the relevant RDS missingness/representation computation as under the person-only condition where ethnicity is not specified.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 ... significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352)”
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the HPSv2.1 row has Latino RDS marked “—”; the value –0.4352 appears in the HPSv2.1 Δ row under Latino PBSG, not Latino RDS.
errors.explanation: The text misidentifies a gender-bias delta value as the Latino ethnicity representation RDS value. Table 5 does not report Latino RDS = –0.4352 for HPSv2.1.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: framework uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification; analysis covers human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases. Sections referenced: framework Section 3/3.3; analyses Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects.

Abstract/intro claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality, fidelity, coherence, controllability, but preference data may encode social/demographic bias; reward models can inherit/amplify this and pass it to aligned video generators. Central question: how alignment tuning influences distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3/3.3) is introduced as a framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It uses event-based prompts, based on social bias taxonomies, to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes. Focuses specifically on gender and ethnicity because they have comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification.

Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants/before vs after alignment, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Claimed results: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Analyses referenced: human preference/reward preference biases in Sec. 5.1/5.2 and downstream video generation biases in Sec. 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training, e.g. reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic reward model. Unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Framework: VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in text-to-video generation using event-based prompts (42 events mentioned later) grounded in social bias taxonomies, separating event semantics from actor identity. Focuses on gender and ethnicity. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes across frames and aggregate. Metrics include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence/consistency across video frames.

Pipeline/experiments: Sec. 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Sec. 5.2 studies inheritance/amplification in image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Sec. 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models, comparing before/after alignment. Sec. 7 constructs controllable/curated image reward datasets by manipulating social attribute distributions and trains reward models to steer video model bias representations.

Claims/results to check later: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models inherit and amplify these biases. Alignment propagates biases into video generators; male-/female-preferred reward models systematically shift gender portrayals, while ethnicity remains uneven. Alignment improves visual quality/coherence and TAS/consistency of social attributes but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Contributions claimed: VideoBiasEval; first end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion; guidance via targeted data composition/counter-biased reward modeling to steer toward equitable behavior.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training (reward/RLHF-style with preference/aesthetic reward models); unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3) evaluates social bias in T2V generation via event-based prompting. Event defined as tuple <p,a,c>: actor p performs verb/action a in context c. It systematically varies actor gender and ethnicity, generates videos, then uses a VLM-based method to extract main character gender/ethnicity across frames and evaluate consistency/fairness at multiple granularities/event categories. Metrics from earlier notes include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS).

Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, neutral “person,” non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. Verbs listed: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Authors state verbs are socially associated with gender/ethnicity stereotypes and visually distinctive for short clips.

Experimental roadmap from earlier: Sec. 5.1 analyzes HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic demographic preferences; Sec. 5.2 reward models HPSv2.0/HPSv2.1/PickScore inherit/amplify biases; Sec. 6 fine-tunes VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model with image reward models; Sec. 7 uses curated reward datasets to steer bias. Key claimed findings to check: preference datasets and reward models favor White/non-neutral gender patterns; alignment propagates biases, shifts gender according to reward model, ethnicity remains uneven; alignment improves quality/coherence/TAS but may stabilize biased depictions.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space... [has] four gender categories” and “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes. Luccioni et al. (2023) supplies man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person...”
errors.evidence: In §3.3 Attribute extraction, the paper defines extracted gender outputs as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}.”
errors.explanation: The paper says the controlled gender attribute space contains four categories, including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual evaluation/extraction label space contains only two gender categories. If these are both describing the audited actor attributes, the definitions conflict.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: The same section says V9R prompts explicitly prepend ethnic descriptors: “An East Asian person is baking...” and “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person’... permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.” Table 1 also states prompts “explicitly contain ethnicity when specified.”
errors.explanation: V9R generation prompts explicitly introduce an ethnicity demographic attribute during generation, contradicting the blanket claim that demographic attributes are not introduced during generation.

errors.claim: “The uniform reference pertains to neutral J7K auditing, whose prompts intentionally remove contextual and identity cues.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “J7K has 42 person-only prompts, one per verb/context” and template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].”
errors.explanation: J7K removes explicit identity cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; each J7K prompt still includes a verb and fixed context.

errors.claim: “N_total = N_man + N_woman” for the gender diagnostic, using only man/woman categories.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “QX2 defines ... bounded attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person).”
errors.explanation: The paper earlier defined four gender categories, but this metric treats gender as only man/woman and defines totals only over those two categories without explaining what happened to neutral and non-binary categories.

errors.claim: “V9R supplies gender assessment, J7K supplies ethnic balance.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “V9R conditions on ethnicity; J7K leaves gender/ethnicity implicit but still includes verb/context” and ethnicity metrics are defined over ethnicity labels. This part’s own Table 2 reports many ethnicity F6N values for White/Black/Latino/etc. while saying J7K has zero recognizable instances for some ethnicities.
errors.explanation: The paper previously defined V9R as the ethnicity-conditioned prompt set, so it is the natural source for controlled ethnicity balance across the seven ethnicities. Saying J7K supplies ethnic balance conflicts with the earlier definition that J7K has no ethnicity specification and with this table’s reliance on ethnicity-specific quantities.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: In Table 2, Southeast Asian F6N and India F6N are ‘—’ for multiple rows, but the same rows report Southeast Asian L2V and India L2V values, e.g. D8P has “Southeast Asian L2V 0.4611” and “India L2V 0.3938.”
errors.explanation: If there are zero recognizable instances for an ethnicity and this prevents subgroup computation, the ethnicity-specific L2V for that same subgroup should also be uncomputable. The table simultaneously marks subgroup absence for F6N while reporting subgroup L2V.

errors.claim: “D8P has the strongest imbalance, worsened in K5X”
errors.explanation: For White overrepresentation, K5X is stronger than D8P; for gender imbalance, B7Q and H4M have much higher Average L2V than D8P. Thus D8P is not the strongest imbalance under either displayed metric.

errors.claim: “Generated videos in full pool | 400 | 400”
errors.evidence: This part also says: “Each prompt is generated 10 times per model with different seeds.” Earlier notes: J7K has 42 prompts and V9R has 294 prompts. Four models are evaluated.
errors.explanation: The stated generation setup implies far more than 400 generated videos in the full pool: even J7K alone would be 42 × 10 × 4 = 1680 videos, and V9R would be 294 × 10 × 4 = 11760. The table’s “full pool” count of 400 conflicts with the paper’s own prompt/model/seed counts unless it is only a validation subset, which it does not say.

errors.claim: “Y2F ... has the lowest diversity”
errors.evidence: Table 4 Overall W3H values: Y2F = 0.8495, A3J = 0.8492, U8D = 0.8470, E5W = 0.8483. Earlier notes define W3H/SDI as diversity where higher is more diverse.
errors.explanation: Y2F has the highest W3H among the listed models, not the lowest diversity. The narrative reverses the direction of the table’s diversity metric.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: Table 4 lists E5W East Asian F6N as 0.0316.
errors.explanation: The additional narrative quantity gives a different value for the same model/ethnicity metric than Table 4.

errors.claim: “C4Z | 1176” prompts, while Figure 5 says “Only [gender]∈{man,woman} appears.”
errors.evidence: V9R has 294 prompts and C4Z is described as adding gender to the same ethnicity/verb/context structure; with only two genders, C4Z would be 294 × 2 = 588 prompts, not 1176. Earlier notes also record C4Z = Ethnicity+Gender and V9R ethnicity alone.
errors.explanation: The stated C4Z prompt count implies four gender categories per V9R prompt, but this part says only man/woman appear.

errors.claim: “Constructed-benchmark images use ‘A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context].’”
errors.evidence: Later in the same part: “generation uses ‘A/An [ethnicity] [gender] is [verb]-ing [context]’ and explicitly fixes all three dimensions.” Table 3 also says prompts contain “verbs, and context.”

errors.claim: “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals. Biases in preference data enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Introduces/uses QX2 for event-based separation of verbs and contexts from actor gender and ethnicity. Measures: ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Claims to be first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but encode/amplify social bias; calls for bias-aware assessment/mitigation throughout alignment. Figure 1 described as showing QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit; frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes; and comprehensive analysis separating human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/introduction claims alignment-tuned video diffusion improves smoothness/fidelity/coherence/controllability but can make portrayals more stereotyped and temporally persistent. Biases in human comparison/preference data enter reward models, are inherited/amplified, and propagate into video generation; learned rewards can systematically redirect gender portrayals, while ethnic distributions remain uneven and White representations are favored. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained after likelihood-based training using reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons; unaligned counterparts use likelihood objectives only as baselines. Introduces/uses QX2, also called VideoBiasEval here, to separate verbs/events and contexts from actor gender/ethnicity. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Measures include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence, using frame-wise VLM inference/aggregation of actor attributes. Claimed contributions: comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit; first end-to-end/connected analysis linking human preference data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape/reinforce social composition; and mitigation/control guidance via attribute distribution curation, targeted composition, and counter-biased rewards.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition ... preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”

errors.evidence: Earlier Table 2 SDI values in the notes are much smaller: ModelScope SDI .0538, InstructVideo .0267, VideoCrafter-V2 .1252, and T2V-Turbo-V1 .1119.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: framework uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification; analysis covers human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases. Sections referenced: framework Section 3/3.3; analyses Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects.

Abstract/intro claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality, fidelity, coherence, controllability, but preference data may encode social/demographic bias; reward models can inherit/amplify this and pass it to aligned video generators. Central question: how alignment tuning influences distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3/3.3) is introduced as a framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It uses event-based prompts, based on social bias taxonomies, to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes. Focuses specifically on gender and ethnicity because they have comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification.

Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants/before vs after alignment, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Claimed results: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Analyses referenced: human preference/reward preference biases in Sec. 5.1/5.2 and downstream video generation biases in Sec. 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training, e.g. reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic reward model. Unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Framework: VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in text-to-video generation using event-based prompts (42 events mentioned later) grounded in social bias taxonomies, separating event semantics from actor identity. Focuses on gender and ethnicity. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes across frames and aggregate. Metrics include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence/consistency across video frames.

Pipeline/experiments: Sec. 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Sec. 5.2 studies inheritance/amplification in image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Sec. 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models, comparing before/after alignment. Sec. 7 constructs controllable/curated image reward datasets by manipulating social attribute distributions and trains reward models to steer video model bias representations.

Alignment propagates biases into video generators; male-/female-preferred reward models systematically shift gender portrayals, while ethnicity remains uneven. Alignment improves visual quality/coherence and TAS/consistency of social attributes but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Contributions claimed: VideoBiasEval; first end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion; guidance via targeted data composition/counter-biased reward modeling to steer toward equitable behavior.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3) evaluates social bias in T2V generation via event-based prompting. Event defined as tuple <p,a,c>: actor p performs verb/action a in context c. It systematically varies actor gender and ethnicity, generates videos, then uses a VLM-based method to extract main character gender/ethnicity across frames and evaluate consistency/fairness at multiple granularities/event categories. Authors state verbs are socially associated with gender/ethnicity stereotypes and visually distinctive for short clips.

Gender output defined as {man, woman}; ethnicity {White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Majority vote over frames gives video-level labels, then ensemble across models. Human–model correlation promised Sec. 4.

TAS: percentage of frames whose classified attributes match final majority-voted video label; high = coherent/stable demographic portrayal, low = flickering/inconsistent identity.

PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total in [-1,1], per verb and ethnicity; positive male bias, negative female bias, zero parity diagnostic not real-world ground truth. Footnote contradictorily says “exclude gender bias from this analysis” while section analyzes gender bias.

Ethnicity metrics: RDSe = Pe - 1/|E|, Pe = Ne/N_total identifiable ethnicity; with 7 groups uniform=14.3%. Example RDS=0.769 => 91.2%. SDI = 1 - sum Pe^2; higher = more diverse/balanced. Bias shift: compute ΔPBSG, ΔRDSe, ΔSDI comparing unaligned vs aligned; improvement = balanced gender, reduced ethnic skew, higher diversity.

Title: “From Preferences to Prejudice...” Aligned = preference/RLHF/reward-tuned video diffusion; unaligned = likelihood baselines. Sec.4 evaluates ModelScope→InstructVideo and VideoCrafter-2→T2V-Turbo-V1; 10 seeds/prompt/model.

Prompt/design inconsistency: Sec.3 said VideoBiasEval varies actor gender/ethnicity with 4 gender categories, 7 ethnic groups, 42 verbs. Later prompt description only Person-only=42 and Ethnicity+Person=294; no explicit gender condition, though later mentions ethnicity+gender. Sec.5.2/Table 3 image reward benchmark: Ethnicity+Person 294; Ethnicity+Gender 1176 (=42*7*4). Fig.5 only gender {man,woman}.

Video judging: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, 16 frames/video. Gender labels {man,woman}; ethnicity 7 groups. TAS=% frames matching final label. PBSG=(N_man-N_woman)/N_total, range [-1,1]. Earlier Table 2 avg PBSG: ModelScope .4815, InstructVideo .5295; VideoCrafter .7581, T2V .8306. Human sensitivity claimed SDI .745→.761 inconsistent with Table 2 scale/values.

Sec.5.1 image reward datasets: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Text/figures also say distributions across 42 verbs. Table 4: Avg PBSG CLIP -0.0726, HPSv2.0 0.6039, HPSv2.1 -0.0984, PickScore -0.1157; one text incorrectly says CLIP +0.0726 man-preference.

Sec.6 VCM-VC2 Table5 SDI: base .1433, HPS2 .1257, HPS2.1 .0976, Pick .1467. Table6: VCM-VC2 baseline ethnicity TAS .8904; HPSv2.1 .9632; gender TAS .9895/perfect .9440. HPSv2.0 PBSG .8034→.9116.

Sec.7: Constructs RMM/RMW from Ethnicity+Gender, 2.94M pairs + 537,660 HPDv2. Table7 calls RMM values “PBSG” but >1 (impossible). Table8 VCM base PBSG .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082, all ethnicities still positive, so RMW reduces male skew but does not produce woman-preference despite text/summary claiming woman-preferred shifts.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Abstract claims: alignment tuning with reward models trained on human preferences improves visual quality but can encode/amplify social biases. VideoBiasEval uses event-based prompts to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. They claim first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Results claim alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: framework uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification; analysis covers human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases. Sections referenced: framework Section 3/3.3; analyses Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Defines aligned models as video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. Unaligned counterparts are likelihood-trained baselines used to isolate alignment effects.

Abstract/intro claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality, fidelity, coherence, controllability, but preference data may encode social/demographic bias; reward models can inherit/amplify this and pass it to aligned video generators. Central question: how alignment tuning influences distributions of social attributes in video diffusion models.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3/3.3) is introduced as a framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It uses event-based prompts, based on social bias taxonomies, to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor identity attributes. Focuses specifically on gender and ethnicity because they have comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames, aggregate for bias quantification.

Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants/before vs after alignment, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claimed first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Claimed results: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Analyses referenced: human preference/reward preference biases in Sec. 5.1/5.2 and downstream video generation biases in Sec. 6.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training, e.g. reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style optimization with learned preference/aesthetic reward model. Unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Framework: VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in text-to-video generation using event-based prompts (42 events mentioned later) grounded in social bias taxonomies, separating event semantics from actor identity. Focuses on gender and ethnicity. Uses VLMs to infer actor attributes across frames and aggregate. Metrics include overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts pre/post alignment, and Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for persistence/consistency across video frames.

Pipeline/experiments: Sec. 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Sec. 5.2 studies inheritance/amplification in image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Sec. 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models, comparing before/after alignment. Sec. 7 constructs controllable/curated image reward datasets by manipulating social attribute distributions and trains reward models to steer video model bias representations.

Claims/results to check later: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models inherit and amplify these biases. Alignment propagates biases into video generators; male-/female-preferred reward models systematically shift gender portrayals, while ethnicity remains uneven. Alignment improves visual quality/coherence and TAS/consistency of social attributes but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Contributions claimed: VideoBiasEval; first end-to-end analysis linking preference datasets → reward models → alignment-tuned video diffusion; guidance via targeted data composition/counter-biased reward modeling to steer toward equitable behavior.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Aligned models = video diffusion models post-trained for human preferences beyond likelihood training (reward/RLHF-style with preference/aesthetic reward models); unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

VideoBiasEval (Sec. 3) evaluates social bias in T2V generation via event-based prompting. Event defined as tuple <p,a,c>: actor p performs verb/action a in context c.
